I've had a number of Bluetooth headphones and the overwhelming majority of them have an "audio interface" that makes sense - some bare bones, some quite pleasant. This interface is in the form of sounds the relate to each of the functions - power on/off, paring, etc. These headphones have a TERRIBLE interface. When you power them on an annoyingly loud series of tones blares in your ear. The tones rise in pitch. When you continue to hold the power button, to access the paring mode, all you hear is an extremely brief, muffled tone. Apparently, the makers thought this was enough of a signal to indicate you're in paring mode. Believe me, it is NOT obvious at all. When you power off the headphones, you hear the same annoying loud series of tones. In this case, the tones do not decrease in pitch, which one might expect.

By comparison, the audio interface of my other Bluetooth headphones are a joy - unfortunately, they do not have volume controls or skip and rewind. When powering them on, a pleasant female voice says, "Hello", and when you enter pairing mode, the same voice says, "Ready to pair." When pairing is established, the voice says, You're connected", then tells me how much charge I have - either full, medium or low. These Cootree headphones do none of that. You'll be lucky if you're able to tell if they've been turned off properly.

In terms of sound quality, they're okay - nothing exceptional. In terms of fit, they're okay as well. Again, nothing exceptional. To my knowledge, they do not have an active noise cancelling function, other than what little noise they may happen to muffle by covering your ears. Let me start by saying I don't use the cell phone features of these headphones, so this review is not all encompassing.

That said, I was a little disappointed in these headphones. Although the sound quality is good, the build quality and attention to detail in design could be better. The control buttons on the right ear are difficult to use as you can't easily feel with your finger where one starts and another begins, You just have to press in the general area, which is not very reassuring. The buttons themselves have no raised symbols or any physical element you can touch to let you know you're on a button, let alone the correct one.

The build quality is not the best. The control buttons fit together less tightly than other Bluetooth headphones I've used. The main play/pause/on/off/pairing button, located in the center of the right earphone in particular seems loose and misaligned.

The functions of the buttons work well enough. However, with some functions, there is no audio feedback. Having used other headsets that provide a short beep each time a button is pressed, I was a little confused when I first tried these - I'd press pause and the audio would just stop, with no beep. I suppose some users would find this preferable though. Some of the button functions, such as play/pause, are not instantaneous. There's a slight delay (about a second) between the time you press it and the time the audio actually plays or pauses. I've experienced this with other Bluetooth headsets and it seems to be a common annoyance.

Because the fit is somewhat tight, getting the earphones on requires a little manipulation. I often find I have to guide the tip of my ear into the space between the neckband (the part that holds the earpieces and wraps around your neck) and the earpiece.This is mainly due to the padding on the earpieces. Once the headphones are on though, they've not uncomfortable. However, a little more space between the neckband and the top of the earpieces would be an improvement. Wearing the headphones lying down or with your head against the back of a seat is not uncomfortable for the most part.

The charging port is has a rubber cover. Although it serves a purpose and some might find this helpful, I find it just gets in the way and will likely fall off. The charging cable is VERY short - about 3 feet, and it comes with no AC adapter, so you'll need to plug it into a USB port for charging - or acquire an adapter so you can use an electrical outlet. Due to the shortness of the cord, it will likely be inconvenient for use with some outlets.

Attaching the charging cord is somewhat difficult. This is to be expected, I guess, due to the micro-USB size of the plug that goes into the ear piece. The end of the cord that plugs into the ear piece is tapered on one side, so there's some visual indication of which way it should go in, but it's always a pain trying to insert these kinds of plugs, no matter what the device. I haven't used the headphones for any great length of time, so I can't comment on the battery life at this time.

The fact that these headphones can fold up to a fairly small size is nice and may be helpful to some when traveling. Typically, I wear them while walking or taking public transportation, so no real advantage for me.

OK, take 2. My original review of this product got hijacked somehow. After writing it, I checked back a couple hours later and my screen name and original title were there, but my review got replaced with what seemed like some guy's journal entry. It had absoluterly nothing to do with this or any other product. Strange.

Anyway - as mentioned in my original posting, this review is more a condemnation or earbud headphones in general than the Sennheiser CX300-B, which I decided to try after my "over ear" style Sony noise canceling headphones went on the fritz. My past experience with earbuds was not good, although I had only ever tried the type that come with the iPod and not the "ear plug" type that go in the ear canal, like the Sennheiser CX300-B. However, having owned a pair of Sennheiser over the ear headphones back in the 70's, my impression of the company and their products was good. So, I decided to take the plunge. What a mistake.

After opening the package (no easy feat - damn sound welded plastic clamshells!), I popped on the medium-sized bud covers (appropriate for my size ears) and inserted them into my ears. I turned on my mp3 player and listened for a few minutes. The sound was adequate - nothing spectacular. I did notice they had decent bass and did block some external noise. I kept listening as I stepped outside to go to the store. I couldn't believe what I heard. Every step I took was amplified in my head - like a booming bass drum. Even the gentle bumping of the cord against my chest was amplified - a constant thump, thump, thump that was impossible to ignore. As it turns out, the very feature that blocks a modicum of external noise, also amplifies any sound that travels through the body. Even breathing is amplified! As I walked, it sounded as though I was listening to someone breathe over a PA system! I had hoped to use these while running, but there's no way that's going to happen. In fact, the problem with amplified sound is so bad, I won't use them at all.

I am very disappointed in this product and will never buy any ear plug style headphones again. I don't understand why anyone would sell them, let alone use them. They may have great sound reproduction, but the listening experience is totally ruined by the sounds that get amplified through the body. It amazes me that people buy similar style products that sell for hundreds of dollars. The only way you can enjoy the sound they produce is to sit perfectly still. I'm glad I only paid about $16 for these things. I won't return them because it'll be too much of a hassle - probably cost more to ship them back than I paid.

BTW - The photo of the product is misleading. The cord looks thicker than it actually is and there's no way it can be coiled as is shown in the photo. It gives the impression the cord is more supple and flexible that it really is. Also, one end of the cord is longer than the other. Not sure why this is, but the thinness of the cord makes it prone to kinking and tangling. In fact, since one side of the cord is longer than the other, it makes it even more prone to tangling.

Bottom line - steer clear of the Sennheiser CX300-B and all ear plug style earbuds.

I bought into the hype and some early favorable 'professional' reviews on this product (and am now convinced the website that posted it was probably paid by Whistler to hype up the release) and purchased it back in late June. I could have easily gotten a similar quality product for much less...or better yet, spent more and got a better, more reliable unit. Convinced that it wasn't working as advertised, I purchased a V1, the 'King' of radar detectors, and compared them in my car side by side. First off, the 78SE gives TONS of false alarms. Often it would go off when the v1 wasn't making a peep. Sometimes, it would go crazy when I was out in the middle of a road surrounded by corn fields! Is this because it is more sensitive? I think not. I had tested them on some speed signs set up in my area, and the V1 would go off a 1/4 mile or more before the Whistler made a detection. A 1/4 mile in the world of radar is an eternity--the difference between getting a ticket and not. By the time the 78SE starting making weak little burps warning you to start being on the lookout, the V1 was already going off at full blast. The v1 would also detect the speed radar when it was up and over a hill--presumably from the minute signature bouncing off different objects alongside the road. Again, not a peep was heard from the 78SE.

I am not saying I expect the 78SE to be as good as a $400 V1. I do, however, expect the performance to be enough to serve its purpose, which is warning you of radar before the cop has your speed. This detector simply won't do that, which makes owning it more or less pointless IMO. The numerous false alerts make you on guard when you don't need to be, and eventually you will simply ignore all the warnings--even the legitimate ones. When the real threats arise, it is doubtful you will know before the cop has your speed--MAYBE it will provide a small benefit in the most optimal conditions (a flat road going perfectly straight)...but how often is that the case? Save your hard earned $$ for a detector that will work...or if your dead set on spending less than $200, do more research and see if you can find something better or at least cheaper!

If you expect things to look like daylight, you'll be disappointed. It is far better than an old Russian unit I have which was an early generation light amplification unit, (green glow type). What you have here is a lot like a B&W security camera with an IR illuminator built into a hand held portable unit.

As some of the other reviews indicate, in the beginning it will seem somewhat cumbersome and clunky getting used to the controls and finding the most pleasing contrast settings. Takes a while, but once you get used to it, it gets a lot easier to make it work like you want it too.

One problem is that if you are just moving around in very low light and want to take a better look at things, it takes time for your eyes to adjust from darkness to the brightness in the viewfinder and then going back. The best way to use it is looking through it for an extended time scanning the area of interest, keeping your eye on the eyepiece. Different types of scenes will take some adjustment to optimize the appearance. Some things reflect light better than others so the best scenario is watching a particular area for an extended period. Once your eyes adjust and you get the contrast dialed in, it works pretty well. The IR illuminators are surprisingly pretty powerful. At short distances the high powered one will "wash out" what you're looking at, but it does seem to reach out pretty good. The claimed 600 feet is a bit of a stretch except under the most ideal of conditions. If you have some ambient light, I think it is better without it. But in really dark country night where you can't see your hand in front of your face, it does a great job of lighting things up.

My feelings on it are mixed. The basic idea of a monocular fits that role of "occasional use" where you want a quick better look at something, but I think that is asking too much from such a device. Plan on spending some time to get a better look at things because your eyes need adjustment time. Once you get the unit dialed in for the scene your watching, it will work pretty well. It's not cheap by any means, but it does work and it's a nice compact package. If you want really high performance night optics, plan on spending a lot more. It will definitely allow you to see reasonable well in darkness, but you have to fiddle with it. A lot has to do with the application. The pros and cons have given me some ideas about building a special purpose device.

Overall, it's a big improvement on some of the early night vision technology. The more I use it, the more I like it and learn tricks about using it effectively. I am happy with it, but for the average person with little experience with night vision, your expectations may not be met and that's why I'm giving it 3 stars. You will need a little patience to go through the learning curve using it.

If you don't brace the frame, you'll just be pulling the entire unit, and you might end up unplugging whatever you have sitting on top. Yes, it is that tight. I tried WD40, but that didn't help. The bottom drawer is worse than the top drawer. Knocking 2 stars for this issue.

THE GOOD:
--------------
* It will do as it says.. capture videos from your sources.
* Video quality seems fine to me. I'm not that picky, the stuff I record isn't important.
* You can install a micro SD card, or connect a hard drive via usb.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Consistent with their products, they cut corners when it comes to the remote control. It's just a terrible clunky experience. I can't even put into words what's wrong with it. I guess there is a delay. So if you're impatient, you'll be pressing too many buttons, and you'll be in the wrong menu, navigate to the wrong places, enable the wrong features, etc. So my advice is to be patient. Press the button you want to press, then wait a week for it to respond. I don't know what inner components make a great remote control. Whatever they are, they are not inside ClearClick remotes. I've reviewed some of their other Clearclick products that are $150 and less, and so I was more forgiving. But at $250, really? You're going to still skimp out on the remote at this price range?

* If you toggle into PLAYBACK mode... good luck getting out of it. Back button doesn't work, and it's always thinking you want to delete files. Everytime I escape playback mode, I'm relieved, but also have no clue how I got out.

* Power on/off is weird. There are scenarios that will make your heart stop because you'll think the device shorted out. Just like their terrible remotes, I've noticed this power issue with their other models too. The quirk is this... sometimes when you power off and on too quickly, it just goes dead. It will not respond for a long time. Don't panic. Stop pushing the power button. Just unplug everything. The hard drive, the HDMI, the power, unplug everything. Go walk your dog, and when you come back, and connect everything again, it will power up. This happens to other Clearclick devices I have, so when it happened with this device, I didn't panic. I knew what was up.

* Power port is micro usb. Again, at $250, I'd like to see USB-C. Micro usb is antiquated, and their cords are prone to get damaged.

* You will need a HDMI splitter to bypass HDCP, as well as be able to turn off your Clearclick when you're not recording, and still watch TV. In my scenario... my source goes into my splitter, and my splitter has TWO outs. One goes into the Clearclick, and the other goes to my projector. This way, I can turn off my Clearclick if I'm not recording, and still watch my projector. If I connect the source directly to the Clearclick, and then go OUT from the Clearclick to my projector, then I would get their ugly icons on my projector. In my pictures, the source is my Nvidia Shield, you'll notice a row of white icons at the top. There is no option to hide these icons in passthrough mode. So if you use the Clearclick as a passthrough, you will get those ugly icons on your big screen. So even if you're recording sources that do not need a HDMI splitter. I'd still get one anyway because using the hdmi passthrough is not pretty. However, the good thing is that the files you record, will not have those icons.

In conclusion, if this weren't a Vine item, I would send it back. Having said all that, it's possible that my expectations may be unreasonable for a very niche product. If a big company like Sony or Samsung create a polished standalone capture device like this, maybe it'd be $500-$600. In which case, you'd be pretty happy with the ClearClick. If you learn to live with the quirks, it's a nifty piece of tech. Hopefully, they can improve on the user experience through firmware updates. I'll go 3-Stars this time.

Very nice high quality item, but you're sort of left in the wind to figure things out yourself. Here are some things to note, so you don't encounter the same issues as I did.

-The app to download is called PRINT MASTER. You'll naturally want to download Phomemo app, but you'll soon realize it won't connect with your printer. Then you'll notice there is a specific Phomemo 110 app, so you download that as well. But after installing this app, a pop up says "we are discontinuing this app, please download PRINT MASTER." There, I saved you from the run-around I encountered. LOL!

-You are given a starter roll of labels, but to use the templates in the Print Master app, you'll need to choose the proper dimension. It would be nice if this info was given in the manual, but the manual doesn't even mention the free roll. Everything is in mm, but I happened to have a mm ruler and measured the labels to be 40x30mm.

-Lastly, the most important advice you need to know is you need to turn on AUTOMATIC. You might ask AUTOMATIC what? My reply is.. EXACTLY. LOL! You see, once you go to print your label. There is a setting called AUTOMATIC. There is no explanation as to what this means. The default is WHITE, which is OFF. What it means is where it will stop after it prints your label. If it's OFF, it will NOT stop. It will continue spitting out blank labels. I saw a YT reviewer who had this issue, and I didn't think anything of it, until it happened to me. LOL! You need to turn this to GRAY, which is ON. It will then automatically stop after it prints your label. Why in the world is the default set to continuously print blanks? We all tend to use default settings because we trust the manufacture knows what's best for us. I mean why would you turn something on if you don't know what it does? So I can see why many make this mistake. But now you know. Turn it on! Even if you need multiple copies, for example 5 copies. You still need to turn it on, so that it will stop after 5 labels. I would love for someone experience with these things, or the seller, to comment below what that setting is for, and why is the default off?

IMPORTANT ADVICE... do not thread the mini ball head onto anything too tightly. This stand is actually fine, it's the cheap ball head that has given me headaches. The ball head has a... I'm not sure what the technical term is for this kind of bolt, but lets call it a "dual bolt." 1/4 bolt is threaded inside a bigger bolt, I presume 1/2. I threaded a mini projector onto this thing, I guess a little too tight. When I unthreaded the projector, the 1/4 bolt was stuck, meaning it was unthreading WITH the projector. So the 1/4 bolt came off the 1/2 bolt. You would think that all it takes are some pliers, but surprisingly, pliers even with teeth, have a hard time gripping this bolt. I had to use my drill press vise to get it off.

To properly use that ball head, you want to thread it onto whatever device you're using, but don't thread it on too tight like me. Then tighten with the lower knob. You might think, this reviewer isn't using common sense. I don't think so at all. Anybody would like his/her electronics threaded securely. The amount of strength I used was reasonable. The issue lies in that inner 1/4 bolt not being secured enough inside that bigger bolt. But I fixed that. Once I was able to unthread the projector from the vise... with the 1/4 bolt now free, but secured by the vise, I then took the ball head body to the vise and threaded the bigger bolt onto the 1/4 bolt a "wee bit" tighter than the manufacturer did.

If you don't have drill press vise like I do, then you better be extra careful using this. 3-Stars.

At $160, I said Nah. At $120, I said let me check this out, and my instincts were right, this is a no-go. Brydge seems to be a legit aspiring company, but I hope they go back to the drawing board and add upper cases to their keyboard design. So that you can put your tablet in a case, then the case connects to the keyboard, a perfect example of this design is an iPad keyboard made by Yoozon, I just reviewed it, it is awesome. There is absolutely no fear of damaging the screen with that type of design. But as for this Brydge keyboard, one word sums up my experience.. uncomfortable.

So there are 3 issues with this design:

1. There is no case, your tablet is exposed. This is not a deal-breaker, I knew it going in. But understand nobody makes any cases for pixel slate. Even Brydge makes a bunch of cases for various ipads complete with slots cut-out so that they can be slide right into their hinge keyboards. But there are no such products for the Slate, so you'll expose it to scatches.

2. Light bleeding in the corner caused by the hinges. I knew this going in as well, but I was thinking maybe it's paranoia. At $120, I wanted to check it out. And honestly, playing with it did not ease my concerns. You don't see any light bleeding at all, but you do see it when you close it like a laptop and the hinge is applying its pressure. I tried to reproduce this light bleed by applying pressure with my thumb, and I could not get it to bleed. So this tells me the hinge is applying a tremendous amount of pressure. Right now, the bleeding goes away the moment it's opened, but by opening and closing constantly and daily, I fear one day the bleeding will stay lit because I've seen this issue on normal laptops.

3. The hinge is a very thin sharp metal. The padding is what prevents it from scratching your tablet. But the padding for one hinge was no longer sticking flush with the metal. It would get caught at times when I'm sliding in the tablet. Good thing I was careful because if you carelessly trust the product, it can scratch your tablet if the rubber gets caught and pulled. Hard to articulate what I'm saying, so I've attached a photo to show you the separation of the rubber from the thin metal hinge. After a couple of uses, it was a chore for me to carefully slide the tablet in because that rubber kept getting caught. A little disappointed that just one day into this testing, I already have to resort to glue?

Like I said... uncomfortable. Brydge, please continue to focus on rigid hinge keyboards. You're on the right path. This is what we want. We want rigidness and lappability, but please design a detachable case so that the case takes the brunt of the hinge pressure, as well as protect the tablet from scratches exactly like the Yoozon design I mentioned above.

Very easy to use this- I set it up in like a minute without even reading the instructions thanks to the on screen prompts. It was very painless.

Sound- it calls the speakers "loud speakers" but some videos I can BARELY hear sound, others I can hear it if everything around me is quiet and that's with the frame's volume turned up to max! Nothing "loud" about this and sadly it doesn't have bluetooth or amy sound output. I guess if you want sound, your best bet is the play music with some other device along with this.

Overall this is a fairly nice, easy-to-use frame. I loaded pictures and videos on it with ease. The speakers need major improvement. The only other complaint is the price point but these frames all seem to be higher priced than a tv which seems silly. You can get a 24 inch tv with a usb slot cheaper than this 15" screen and it'd probably have better picture. For the price, It should have much better viewing angles/ better video quality.

It works and everything on it is just ok quality. It feels like something you'd buy at the dollar store, it's so light and cheap looking. I don't expect it to last forever but if you need a cheap camera for now, it'll work.

So the picture on these cameras is AWFUL. The app is extremely slow to load and it's a crappy app- you can't record video or get video clips even without paying for a subscription. So without paying a monthly fee, literally all you can get is the ability to se a live stream. And even that is awful due to the SLOW loading app and horrible quality image.

In comparison- you can grab a Wyze at a fraction of the price and they record in amazing detail. Plus their app loads instantly, records video clips and puts them into the app (for free) AND you can put a micro sd card into them so you can record events without subscribing to their service. You can access these files from the app even- it's extremely convenient!

Even for what I pay in taxes on these Arlo cameras, I'm extremely disappointed because they're taxed at such a high rate that I could have outright bought Wyze cams and I'd have had much more usable cameras. As is I've ditched the Arlo doorbell camera and put a Wyze one in it's place. I also ordered an outdoor Wyze rechargeable camera to replace this crappy Arlo spotlight model. You couldn't pay me enough to take another Arlo camera, they're horrible!

Overall I don't recommend it at all, there are much better tablets out there available at this price point like the Fire ones.

I am torn when it comes to this smartwatch. First, you track everything through an app on your phone, which I like a lot better than just the watch itself. I can keep up with everything on the app and see my progress and how my blood pressure, steps, heart rate, and all that stuff is doing over the course of months. It helps to see the changes and non-changes. I love that and more smartwatches need these types of details. The major problem I have with this smartwatch though is the actual watch itself. You are supposed to be able to swipe through the different things on the watch but you literally can't most of the time. You have to press down so hard and hope that it swipes but usually, it doesn't and you have to keep trying and trying. It's so freaking annoying and complete trash. It's just a high tech watch that you can't use for anything else that it says you can use it for. Such as taking pictures, using it as a remote, and even control your music from the watch. I have managed to get to the program on the watch but unable to use it because of not being able to swipe or use the watch at all. Oh, and there is only one button on the watch itself, which controls the power and turning the light on and off. That's it, doesn't control anything else. So while I am super impressed with the app and all the functions this offers the watch is freaking useless itself. It does, however, track your steps, heart rate, blood pressure, and even how long you sleep, but don't expect to see much of these through the watch itself but mainly through the app. Such a disappointment.

I had to leave this in my garage for a few days due to the odor. I like the phone photo lens adapter. but it does need to be adjusted 'just so' to get a good photo. The tripod is okay. Only the Monocular Telescope will fit into the nylon bag. The small tripod and phone adapter do not fit in the bag. The lens caps do not have a security tie, one is loose and the other is attached to the rim of the monocular end, so you really have to press it away from the lens view to see unobstructed. You can remove the little strap on the middle of the bottom and mount it onto any 1/4 tripod mount, so that makes it a little more versatile.

This isn't 80x100 magnification, I find it to be about half of that at best. There is no 'night vision' this is just a monocular telescope that is nice for watching wildlife, or for use in nature... or spying on your neighbors.

I cannot say I find this to be a good value, nor is it terrible. There are some pros and cons that will vary from user to user. There is room for some simple improvements. The odor is very strong out of the package. The included instruction care card is of limited use as the translation is poor. Both of the lens cap covers could stand to be attached via a nylon braided cord and it would be nice if the nylon bag could hold the accessories as well.

Thank you for reading my review. I hope you find it helpful and will click the Helpful button below.

I really wanted to use this. I absolutely hate this tripod. I own several. Upon extending the legs to set it up, it broke and I cannot fix it. There are these little thin, plastic tabs inside each piece of tubing that extends. The washer came off, the plastic tabs went flying, I placed them back, and the leg was stuck. I tried to retrieve them to try placing it again, and they were lost in the larger section of tubing. I carefully and methodically removed the larger washer to find the tabs, and they were so far up inside I couldn't retrieve them, so I replaced the plastic tabs from the larger piece, carefully placed it back... and low and behold those disappeared inside as well.

This is the worst engineered product I have ever encountered in my life. I cannot fathom paying anything for this. It's worthless garbage to me now. It cannot be used. I feel sorry for all the people that spent precious time of their life designing, manufacturing, selling and shipping this piece of trash. An entire tripod leg will no longer fix into place, because of these thin plastic tabs. Maybe this could have been saved by threading the adjustment washers differently, or even a piece of tape holding the plastic tabs. I cannot say for sure. What I can say is, this would be a waste of money. It's much too easy to unscrew the washers, then those tabs come out. They cannot be placed back. Once they are inside the tube, they are gone.

If I can somehow manage to fix this, I will update. Until then, don't waste your money. I would not even recommend this to someone I don't like.

When I first purchased my 3 TB MBL some time ago I was quite pleased. Network access, remote access, even an android app. In short, everything my DLink had plus the app and a nicer look on the shelf. I used it extensively for pulling up photos on my cell phone when I was bored as well as to store my most important files. I didn't back them up, a back-up drive is something I kept saying I would add later...

14 months later (note the 12 month warranty had just expired) the drive stopped being accessible over the network. I spent a week and at least 40 hours of my time going back and forth with tech support by e-mail and trying every option they could offer, and the result was that they deemed the unit broken. They said that the unit can not be opened because that would break the drive inside, and they said that they can't fix it. They "kindly" offered me a referral to one of several companies that give them a kick back for data recovery services. Incidentally, I asked two for pricing by e-mail and they didn't respond.

So I took the unit apart and bought a new unit and took that one apart and swapped the drives. Neither one worked. After talking to support again it turns out that WD didn't want these to be upgradable because if they were upgradable you could buy a cheap drive instead of a new unit so they code each board to the drive that will be in it. TO make matters worse, they encoded the drive in a Linux format that no known version of Linux can translate. Attaching it to my Linux system I couldn't mount it using any utility. Several Linux recovery programs couldn't do anything either.

Okay, having told you why I will never buy a WD NAS again, I should now tell you how to fix this if you have the same problem that I do: DiskInternals makes a program called Linux Reader. That's right, Linux can't read the drive but a program designed to read Linux drives from within Windows can! Recovering the data to a drive is time consuming though. I tried it all at once but that froze after a few days. Then I tried one major directory at a time and that worked better. But recovering nearly 3 TB of data has taken a very long time! I'm about 3 MONTHS into the recovery effort and I have about 400 GB remaining. After starting on my wife's computer because mine is a laptop and causing a few crashes and a lot of delays I finally had to pull out an older computer and set it up just to run this program.

If anyone has the same problem and can't get this solution to work, I'll do my best to help if you simply reply to this review and give me all the details. If anyone is considering buying a WD NAS, I want to encourage you to buy a DLink model 323 (I think the 325 is the current version but it is missing some features so I'd get an older one) instead. I've had that thing running for 5 years without a glitch!

Okay, there are three types of devices which are this size. One is an ebook reader. If that's all you want, get a Paperwhite. Seriously, try reading on the Fire's screen for half an hour and it will be like reading on a computer screen (not so good for the eyes). Especially in low light!

The second is a tablet, if that's what you want then get a Galaxy Tab. I have a Toshiba Thrive, which is similar to the Tab (one step down in some respects, the same in others) and that blows this out of the water in terms of what it can do and how it does it. But it isn't the best at playing back movies. eBook capabilities are similar and screen is similar, so if you aren't going to watch movies on it then DO NOT BUY A FIRE HD!!!

The third type of device I call a portable media device. And here is where the Kindle Fire really shines. The screen is currently the best screen available on a 7" device. And the sound is great. Using the built in application, I can play movies ripped from DVDs with great sound and video. On my Thrive I have trouble with this, getting jittery video and low sound most of the time and no consistency. A free program will convert your videos over to Kindle Fire screen size and save them in a format that the Fire can open (search for them, there are many and lots of free options so don't pay for that).

The negatives are, however, many. The Kindle Fire HD sports the UGLIEST user interface I have ever seen. Some replacements are available, and I'm debating them just like I am debating rooting the device to get the Play store. Note that if you have an Android phone, without rooting you can not get your paid apps on the Fire. Also, you can access only a few thousand of the half a million apps that other Android devices offer. This is just because Amazon wants to reduce piracy by restricting apps that may get around protections, but it costs hundreds of thousands of legitimate apps. Also, Google apps are not present (except gmail), so you can't get Google Maps or Voice or the like without sideloading or rooting. I'm not sure why Amazon hates Google, since Google gave them the framework for this tablet! I got the $25 screen protector and I don't like the feel, but that isn't the tablet's fault.

If you have kids, Amazon's kidtime app is great. Other similar apps are available for other devices, and if you want any content this one costs $2.99/month for a one child license, but it is a good app and they did a great job of integrating it so there are no bugs which could cause your kid to find their way out accidentally (or on purpose for those smarter kids out there). If the service was free for Prime members, or if a limited version was free for Prime members, I would rate this app as 5 stars and perhaps raise the entire Kindle Fire HD up a star since that would add one great use which I currently am not taking advantage of.

Oh, and there is no SD slot, no USB slot for external drives, and no IR port so it can't be a remote control (all very disappointing).

Having said all of that, I am keeping mine for movie playback and occasional reading when on a plane or in a doctor's office. I have a 10" tablet which I love and wouldn't trade in for this Kindle if they paid me. But since I can have both (thanks mostly to putting several people together to buy me one present together), this is worth keeping.

Cons: If you have Carbonite back-up service, if you have a WD MyBookLive NAS, or if you know how to configure any of the several dozen software packages that do this for you, then you can already do this for free without buying this device. Yes, I do mean that there are free packages (at least for Android phones) which you can download and use to make your computer into this device without any fees whatsoever. So for anyone who is mid-level or above in computers, this is not a worthwhile purchase.

Let me start by saying that if you happen to be looking for a way to record music from one of the 41,000 radio stations that this company supports and then take it to your car without having to record it yourself and put it on an mp3 player, it does work.

That being said, the stations are not very inclusive. This isn't going to be XM radio we're talking about. most of the stations are non-US stations (which is a good thing for some people, but not what I was looking for). I wanted children's music for my kids to listen to. I love XM's Kids Place Live, and I wanted something like that. What I found was less than a dozen channels, only 4 in English, and at the time that I set this up all 4 were playing music that wasn't appropriate for my kids. So I decided to move on to pop and use it for myself. This was even harder. There were about 100 top 40 channels, mostly not in English again, and the ones that were were just random stations like 94.9 FM in Nashville, TN (I couldn't tell anything from the names and there is no way to get user reviews of the stations). So I picked one at random and decided to record it just to write the review and then I can add this to the pile of gadgets that I don't use anymore.

That wasn't easy either. You have to start it recording, let it go for the amount of time that you want (this isn't mp3 downloading where you can get a few hours in a few minutes), and make sure your computer doesn't go to sleep. Also, the station dropped out after about 20 minutes and when I came back 4 hours later I discovered that the software doesn't reconnect you automatically, so you really have to use this to listen to music at your computer and then replay the same music in the same order in your car.

The device is also missing features that I just assumed it would have like identifying when songs start and stop to separate tracks, identifying the music and labeling the tracks so I know what I am listening to, or the ability to mark a song at the unit while I am playing it back and later be reminded to go buy that song.

The device was very easy to set up, despite the fact that my 64 bit version of Windows doesn't support their 64 bit client and I had to run the 32 bit version (not a big deal just not sure why they bothered to include the 64 bit version if it doesn't work). I updated to the latest software quite easily as well.

This is a buyer beware situation. The device works as advertised, but has no bells and whistles that aren't mentioned in the product description (like auto-reconnect, which I would consider a standard part of this device's operation). And it is easy to use (if you don't mind baby sitting it). But you can access 100 times that many radio channels online and record them using free software that will do these other things and then download them to your mp3 player in minutes (assuming that you have one, if not check out the Samsung ones and remember to get one with speakers if you will ever want that capability, don't waste your money on a Zune or an IPod unless you have a good reason to).

For me, the product was a free test product, so I didn't waste anything. but I would be returning this if I had paid for it.

I've purchased quite a few compact computers previously and all of them have little quirks that I have to deal with but in the end, I'm able to set them up with the necessary drivers and use them without issues. This Kamrui CK 10, though...

On paper, the specs of this computer is impressive. A 10th generation i7 processor with the integrated Intel graphics which I already knew wouldn't be winning any awards in the gaming department but that's expected. With 16 GB of ram and 512GB of nvme storage, this computer is a good starting point for anyone who needs a fairly powerful PC in a compact package.

Regarding the ram: I've disassembled this computer and found that the ram is soldered to the motherboard, as is the CPU. This means there is no way to upgrade the ram.

Regarding the storage: There is good news here. There are two M.2 slots supporting NVME so SSD storage is quite expandable. I installed another 512gb ssd in the secondary slot.

The operating system that was included was a vanilla Windows 11 Pro with absolutely no additional bloatware aside from what Microsoft has already included. This is good. All drivers were installed and the machine booted fine.

So in my case, it is customary for me to install Windows from scratch when I buy a new computer. It's just something I do. I don't trust that there are no hidden software in the preinstalled systems. As such, I needed to locate the necessary drivers for this computer.

As expected, Windows will successfully detect the graphics, wifi and bluetooth hardware. Also as expected, the Intel chipset drivers needed to be installed manually. All standard so far. With all of this done, there were three pieces of hardware that were unidentifiable. These were the sound drivers.

Scouring the search engines, I couldn't find the drivers for the CK 10. I finally located Kamrui's facebook page, which led to a linktree that then led me to their forums. In the forums, I searched and found a set of drivers for the CK 10. Unfortunately, that seems to be for the CK 10 with an i5 cpu. It did not contain the correct drivers for the sound card.

I resorted to searching for the drivers by device id. From there, I pieced together the necessary drivers to get sound working. I had to use drivers from three different driver sets from HP.

I did reach out to Kamrui's support email. They responded two days later but rather than read what I wrote, they responded with a canned form for me to list my product, serial, purchase date, etc.

So what else is wrong? Well, at least twice per day, this computer freezes without warning. It could be caused by the sound drivers that I had to piece together but how would I know? I don't can't actually get the right drivers for it.

The TROND Flat Plug Power Strip Surge Protector is a great concept. Everything about it shows that some thought has been given to its design. Unfortunately, their choice of materials weren't as well thought out.

Some design concepts that attracted me to this surge protector is that it gives you 8 power plugs in a surface area that's just under 4 x 4 inches. The four plugs at the top are grounded while the 4 on the side are two-prongs. In addition, the wall plug is flat, giving you a lot of options as to where you can plug this product in. Finally, there are three USB-A ports and one USB-C port.

However, as I've mentioned, some design choices are questionable. As with many surge protectors, the USB ports are under-powered. The Type-A ports are not too bad at 5V/2.4A, but there is no quick charge capability. The Type-C is not PD, so your charging options are no better than the Type-A ports. You're stuck with 5V/3A with a total wattage shared between them at 14W or 3.4A.

My second gripe is with the build material. Compared to many power strips, the plastic covering this product feels quite cheap. It has a smooth texture and just feels... thin to the touch. The same plastic also covers the wall plug. In addition, the power wire is thinner than other power strips that you'll find. They feel more like the two-prong extension cords, except that it has three wires.

Now, I don't have proof that their choice of materials will be an issue at all, but it does give me pause.

You can connect up to 2 bluetooth devices to this transmitter and both will be able to hear the audio.

I picked up this transmitter to replace another transmitter because the 1mii has volume controls that is missing from the other transmitter and dedicated buttons to pair headset 1 and 2. To address this, I actually had to install a volume plugin for Chrome which will boost youtube audio by over 200%. Unfortunately, I can't do the same for my other applications. To clarify this a little bit. I pair this device with an open ear bone conduction headset so that I can hear my surroundings while having the computer audio also in my ears. I can certainly put in an earplug to get better sound, it would defeat the purpose of using the open ear design when working at my computer.
