Traveling with electronics is inevitable and when traveling abroad, it's necessary to understand a few things about the places you will be traveling to. Language, currency, electrical standards, and cell phone bands being a few of them. Traveling to the UK or Europe, 220v is the electrical standards. To deal with this, you must understand the electronics that you will be bringing with you. Most modern electronics such as cell phone and laptop chargers will work fine at 220v with a plug adapter (make sure you check the power adapter regarding input voltage), but personal electric devices such as hair dryers and maybe electric shavers might not. There are two choices here. Look for hair dryers that have a switch to allow 220v or 110v. Otherwise, purchase a voltage converter.

The BESTEK 2000W Travel Voltage Converter power strip is one of the more powerful voltage converters that I've seen. Most voltage converters will not support hair dryers because they don't output enough amps for the devices to work. At 2000W, this voltage converter power strip is powerful enough to power most dryers out there (many work at 1800w). This device is well labeled to reduce any confusion. There are two output sockets. One rated at 200w for less intensive devices such as the electric toothbrush and my camera's battery charger. The other socket outputs the full 2000w. This is good for the hair dryer.

I was disappointed that this device doesn't work in the UK and since their standards are a little different from the EU, I didn't want to even try using a plug converter to try it. There's no guarantee as to what wattage the plug converter can handle so it's better to play it safe. Use this device only in the European countries and the others that are listed on this web page.

For me, I didn't take any chances with it. Since the USB ports are fairly standard at 2.4a output but no quick charge or type-c PD, I charged my phones using a different, more robust phone charger. I used this power strip only for the hair dryer with nothing else plugged in. Even then, I don't know that this thing can handle running the thing for too long.

In the end, I think the better strategy is to purchase devices that are rated for both 110v and 220v to save yourself some headache. I was able to find a third-party oral-b electric toothbrush charger rated for 220v and a travel hair dryer with the 220v switch. I'll still have this power strip with me for my camera until I can find a third-party charger for it.

I love the concept of this drive. In fact, I love the concept of drive enclosures with multiple functions (I had an enclosure that was also a portable router). This M.2 NVME Enclosure is a USB hub and memory card reader all-in-one without being any bigger than a standard NVME enclosure.

I love the tool-less design of this enclosure. A single button press allows you to slide the aluminum case open to insert the drive. To secure said drive, there are three cleverly designed clips (see my uploaded images). If your drive is shorter, you will use the first or second clip, but if your drive is the 2280 size, your drive will simply push down the first two clips and snap into the third.

Drive access speed is comparable to my other enclosures and the memory card reading feature works well.

Unfortunately, I had a couple of problems with my enclosure. Firstly, it did not work with my 1tb drive at all. It just wouldn't mount. It did work with my 512gb drive, but I found that the drive would disconnect after about 1 hour of being connected to my computer. Please check your product thoroughly while you're in your return period.

The Wavlink N300 Wi-Fi Range Extender is a quick and easy way to extend your 2.4gHz network to reach the remote corners of your house. It is easy to set up if you're familiar with normal router setup procedures (connect to its wifi or via ethernet cable, then access the router configuration through a browser). It will normally create a wifi SSID that's different from your original wifi, but you can just force it to use the same name.

For my phones and computers, I use my 5G wifi network but the older 2.4 Ghz is great for home automation products such as switches, doorbells, and cameras. Keeping those devices separate from your main network will keep your main network running smoothly and free up a lot of IP addresses on that network.

This device is very stable once it is set up. My IOT devices have been able to communicate at a good speed and have not lost connections yet.

Unfortunately, this extender did not automatically connect with my main router again when I rebooted it. In fact, I was forced to reset the device and set it up all over again in order for it to work. I can't say for sure that the problem is caused by this device or by my main router. It's just my personal experience. Perhaps test this functionality while you're still in your return period for the product.

Just as my title says, this 100 Inch Front and Rear Projector Screen is an acceptable projection screen for backyard movie nights but not great for indoor use.

It is a large piece of white, stretchy cloth that can be tricky to set up. Without a frame, you would need to figure out a way to stretch the screen taut without it sagging too much in the middle and you need to have these hooks set up well in advance of your event because it can take some time. Once you have a good setup for it, the screen is easy to hook up and stow away. It will fold nicely without leaving any creases the next time you need it again.

When used indoors, you will find that this screen leaks a lot of light through to the back wall because it is made to also be a rear projection screen and because of that you're probably losing a lot of the light that should be reflecting back to you. That's why I say that I don't think it works any better than a painted wall when used indoors.

The price of this screen is pretty low but just be sure you know what you're getting into with this screen or you'll just be disappointed.

Bone conduction headphones have become quite popular and because of this, there are many to choose from. This specific model is quite minimalist. A thin metal frame with the vibration units and electronics hanging off it.

In terms of comfort, there is no adjustability to the metal frame so it may take some getting used to because the frame may feel like they are too big or too small depending on your head size. For me it felt a little bit loose but I came to realize that it actually stayed where you place it and it really wasn't a problem.

For sound quality, this bone conduction headphone will never match a nice pair of over-ear headphones but that really isn't what it's for. By leaving the ears open, one is still able to stay aware of the surroundings, making it great for cycling and jogging where hearing the traffic is essential for safety reasons.

A pair of earplugs are included with this product and with one or both in, one can really appreciate the difference between regular headphones and bone conduction. You can still hear the music (or in my case, audiobook) through the earplugs because of the bone vibration but all outside sound is cut off. This means that you'd be able to listen to music over the sound of a loud machine.

I have tried a few different pairs of bone conduction headphones and these are the ones that I have stuck with so far. The buttons maybe be somewhat limited (just two buttons that control volume and power), but they are easily reachable and not hard to press and the IPX6 means it's water resistant against rain and sweat.

I love GL.iNet. All of their routers can run on either their own openwrt with added custom UI and ease-of-use packages or you can install their provided barebones openwrt. You can even download and install the firmware directly from Openwrt.org if available.

With that said, the GL-AX1800(Flint) WiFi 6 Router is a disappointing product. In the last year, Openwrt has made setting up a mesh network of routers using 802.11r and 802.11s but only if you're running version 19.07 or higher. I wanted this router in the hopes that I can upgrade to WIFI 6 for my custom mesh network but I was sad to find that the variant of the firmware is based off version 15.

While gl.iNet has backported all of the necessary security patches from the newer kernels, it won't help the many power users who have come to depend on the new Openwrt version.

Due to this, I didn't give this a thorough test to figure out its stability and wifi speed as both of these can be affected when/if the company finally updates the firmware to a more recent version. Meanwhile, this router will sit in my closet waiting for its day to shine.

These bone conduction headphones are waterproof (IP68) and come with 16GB of storage so that they would work while swimming (bluetooth will not work well under water and really doesn't have the distance to cover a pool). They can be fairly loud and can be heard even with (especially with) earplugs.

The advantages of an open-ear, bone conduction headphone is that you can hear everything going on around you while still being able to listen to your music or audiobook. Put earplugs in your ear and you can retreat into a more private listening experience.

The disadvantage is that the sound quality is just not going to be as good as headphones that cover your ears. That is especially true for this pair of headphones.

The sound quality from these headphones is not good. The lows are barely audible most of the time and when you turn up the volume to try and hear more of the lower tones (including human voices), the higher tones are already too loud. This is alleviated by putting in earplugs. The plugs will block most of the higher tones as those come out of the speakers themselves while the low tones come in through the vibrations.

Another issue I have is that the buttons are horrible. They are made of a single piece of rubber on the outside and the buttons themselves are recessed pretty far in. This means that I have to push quite far before actually hitting the button and there is just no tactile response to know that I've actually pressed it. This makes everyday use of these headphones a chore.

The last problem I have with it is the custom charging cable. I really do not like devices that do this. Not only do you have to remember to bring the cable with you if you need to charge in your car or elsewhere, if it breaks, you're pretty much screwed.

For the price they are charging (more than Aftershokz Titanium), this really isn't worth it.

The only thing these headphones have going for it is a respectable battery life. Everything else is just a disappointment, unfortunately.

I've been trying to find a good but affordable pair bone conduction headphones because I keep a headphone on my head almost all day while I work and write my code but I end up shutting the rest of the family out and miss half of the conversations going on in the house. When I discovered open ear bone conduction, it seemed to be the perfect solution.

So far, I have not found a good one. The specific problems of this pair of headphones is that it is not bone conduction. It is a simple pair of speakers set next to your ear. There is no bone shaking going on. With bone conduction, you can put in earplugs and still hear the audio fairly clearly, with these, the sound is clearly muffled and hard to make out.

In addition, there is a half-second delay on these headphones meaning they are no good for watching videos. I have not experienced bluetooth delay in quite a few years so I wasn't expecting it. Further, there is no charging light, meaning there is no way to tell if they are charged or not.

Then there's the price they are charging for this thing. Everything is just NO.

I received my Tayogo Wireless Bone Conduction Open-Ear Headphones this morning and used it the entire day. While the sound quality isn't as good as a true on-ear headphone or earbuds, the advantage of a bone conduction headphone is the ability to keep your ears open to your surroundings. It was exactly what I needed.

It was a little bit odd to feel the bass vibrating my head at first, but I soon got used to it. I really did like this style of headphones.

At the end of the night, I plug the headphones in and I see the charging light come on. A couple of seconds later, it goes off and from then, I couldn't get any response from the headphone at all. No matter how long I try to hold the power button, it just won't turn on.

I realized that I forgot to first turn off the headphones before plugging it in. I believe that may be what caused the problem.

Quite disappointed to have a device work only for 1 day.

The Samsers Wireless Portable Folding Keyboard is only 1/2" thick when folded, and of course, half that when undfolded. It is quite thin and portable. It caught my attention because it supports pairing with up to 3 bluetooth devices simultaneously and with many of us having multiple devices (phone and tablet is quite normal), these devices are great for someone like me.

The clamshell design means that the keys are protected when closed. It also holds itself closed magnetically, and powers on my simply opening it. Pairing is easy: hold the function key and press one of the Q,W, or E keys to select one of the three bluetooth slots, then press the big "connection" button on the left bezel of the keyboard. This all seems pretty slick to me but I did have one concern with this keyboard's design and that is the hinge system. When the keyboard is open, it is quite easy to twist it with just a little bit of pressure. It means that I'm always extra careful when I'm taking it out of my bag.

In terms of functionality, the keys are a the same size as the ones on my laptop and has the same amount of travel as well, although they are a little bit louder than my laptop's keys when typing. I'm using this keyboard to type this review right now. What I found is that the keys are a little bit unresponsive. I keep missing letters every few words I type. Just in this last sentence, I had to go back about 5 times to correct missing letters. This defeats the purpose of purchasing a keyboard to type more quickly on a mobile device. Perhaps if you are normally heavy-handed when you type on a keyboard, you wouldn't face this issue.

Something that I wish this keyboard had is a touch pad. If this device can be both a keyboard and mouse, it would be much more useful.

Overall, the Samsers Wireless Portable Folding Keyboard is a good device but ultimately, it has a couple of shortcomings that keep it from being great.

In the last few months, I collected a few tripods in various form factors and all of them supported the 1/4 inch quick release mechanism except for one. It was my main tripod, which had the traditional panning arm. It sported the square tripod mount.

I purchased the ZweiFuch Mini Ball Head to convert that tripod to the same quick release so that I can use my mirrorless with all of my tripods without changing plates.

What I found with the ZweiFuch was that it wasn't very convenient to use. The ball head is quite tight, which some may prefer, but I think it really should be able to be loosened more. The bubble level is placed to the side of the mount plate, facing vertically, meaning it is only useful for vertical pictures. There isn't a second bubble sitting flat on the face of the mount.

Of course, I expected this, but without a pan arm, it means that there is a small functionality loss to being able to quickly pan, then tighten it down again. It's just that added to the other problems I had with this ball head, I just don't think it's worth it.

Taking it out of the box, you'd find that the LUXCEO light tube has good build quality. It is all-plastic, but that's much better than the fluorescent tubes of the past. The light is nicely sealed to be water proof and with a 1/4" screw hole on one end, it is easy to set up. A loop on the other end means this tube can be hung via a hook for additional mounting options.

In use, though, I realized that the Achilles heel of this product is in its lack of versatility. I agree with the other top reviews for this product that this light has limited functionality and the reason is because of its simplistic controls. While I normally prefer physical buttons that have specific uses rather than having to take out my phone to control something, the design of the remote control is such that there are only 8 colors to choose from (as seen from the picture). Without the ability to fine-tune the colors, you're really stuck. I think that unless you have a specific liking to the available colors, you'll end up using this as a white light for simply photography or video setups.

There is a single button on the light tube and its operation is as confusing as it is useless. Click on the button and it toggles on and off. Double clicking will cycle through various modes (R, G, B, white, yellow, flashing, etc). Hold the button and it will adjust the brightness.

To further confound the consumer, this light tube comes with a felt bag that fits the tube very well, but nothing else. Not even the remote control, meaning you'll need to find a solution for keeping the remote and tube together.

So in conclusion, this review is for the Luxceo P7RGB. Looking on Amazon, I see that there is Luxceo has a P7RGBPro that costs only $4 more which has a smartphone app to allow full control over the light's colors. It's fairly obvious which you should pick.

The WD_Black 1TB D50 Game Dock has quality written all over it. Metal construction for heat dissipation, thunderbolt support, nice RGB lighting, and a fast NVMe drive. It is quite obviously geared toward the PC Gaming crowd, but which segment?

The build of this product screams high-quality gaming accessory. Its outer design is reminiscent of a cargo container and its collection of ports are impressive. Each USB port is well labeled with its speed (4x 10Gb/s Type-A and 2x 10Gb/s Type-C), two thunderbolt ports, one of which outputs 87 watts of power, one displayport, one network port (gigabit), and one 3.5mm headphone jack. Add to this, the 1TB high-performance NVMe drive. All in one sleek-looking, compact container (pun intended).

It is obvious that this dock is geared toward the Gaming Laptop crowd, whether its for gaming or for video/graphics production work, but I find that it really doesn't make sense for me. In my tests, this product does not work without the power adapter (it really should be able to power itself through the thunderbolt port). This means an additional outlet that's drawing power at all times. This would make sense if gaming laptops can actually be powered and charged from the 87w thunderbolt port but I have not seen a gaming pc with discreet graphics that actually accepts anything in that range.

So what other advantage would this product provide? External storage through a fast Thunderbolt connection. At $450, this product provides 1TB of additional storage. Which 2TB NVMe drives available for much less, I would opt to upgrade my internal storage to 2TB instead.

Then that leave the docking station. The ports are all of the high quality and your monitor, network, keyboard, mouse, headset, and speakers can be connected via a single thunderbolt connection. This is convenient, but I don't think this justifies the price as there are many docks out there that work just as well, albeit through a USB 3.1 connection instead.

WD has really done well to package a lot into this dock but is charging a premium for it. Personally, I think that there are just better ways of achieving equal or better results when it comes to upgrading a gaming laptop.

**update**
Coming back to think about it some more, I realized exactly what niche WD was going for: Macbooks. Some Macbooks have only two thunderbolt ports and all of them are not easily upgradeable so this product does indeed provide a value to those consumers. But then does it make sense to spend an additional 35% of the price of the laptop (Macbook Pro 13" is $1299) to address problems that Apple introduced into their laptops? I guess if you're already in their ecosystem, it's par for the course. That's not to say Apple is the only one. Microsoft has made their products impossible to upgrade as well, but none of these are actually gaming laptops.

This is a fairly standard surge protector with 12 outlets with only two of those set apart for the larger adapters. The selling point that it attempts to sell consumers on is the usb ports, including one type-c so this review will concentrate mostly on those ports.

As far as the surge protector portion of this product, the face outward, which means that the longer style chargers that comes with some electronics will not plug in without taking up an extra socket. With only two set farther apart for power adapters, this power strip will not work well for a location with routers, modem, and NAS.

Now on to the USB ports. Five USB ports share a total of Five amps. It means that is the power strip is completely filled, it will only deliver one amp to each port. The type-c port is only useful if that is the only cable you can find because it does not support any fancy features such as quick charging or type-c pd, although it does support up to 3A so some phones may actually consider this "fast charging". Do not expect to replace a true 5-port usb charger with this power strip.

I needed a router that was confirmed to run Openwrt so I jumped on the opportunity to test the Cudy WiFi 6 Router AX1800 Smart WiFi Router.

At AX1800, this router really isn't much of an upgrade from the AC1750 Archer C7 that I had previously so in terms of WIFI performance, it wasn't much of an upgrade despite it being Wifi 6.

For me, the important factor here is the Openwrt firmware. The default firmware that is installed on the X6 router seems to be a custom skin for LUCI (verified by the URL of /cgi-bin/luci in the browser), but many features are missing in the UI, including the ability to enable ssh, so one of my first actions was to download the Openwrt Firmware from Cudy's website. The following is what I found:

Using the Archer C7 as my main router, I was able to put together a WIFI mesh with fast switching with Openwrt's 802.11r and 802.11s support. I was hoping that I can extend that mesh with the Cudy X6. What I discovered of the Openwrt firmware is that it is a custom compile of the 20.2 branch and therefore, not quite a stable release. After installing the wpad packages to allow 802.11s and WPA3, the wireless drivers didn't work correctly. Without going into too much detail, I believe that the drivers for the Wifi 6 adapter needs some work.

Hopefully, Cudy continues to work on the firmware and incorporate their changes into the official Openwrt repo. Once these problems are ironed out, it be a good replacement for the Archer C7 but even then, don't expect AX1800 to be a revolutionary step up from your current 802.11a wifi. This is the lowest Wifi 6 level that one can purchase.

The NexHT 1080P Pan Digital Tilt / 8X Zoom Indoor Smart Camera has all of the features that one would want from a wifi camera. Panning, recording, remote viewing, infrared night vision and two-way audio. It is also very small. Designed to look like the Wyze cam, it is actually much smaller at 1.5" wide and 3" tall. While cloud storage services are available, there is a microsd port for local recording.

If one just needs a basic camera at a low price to monitor the home, this camera will serve well. To compare to products such as Wyze, this camera comes up a little bit short. The title of the product is carefully worded to show that the tilt function is "digital", which really means that the camera records with a wide-angled lens and when the phone is held in landscape mode, one can drag the image up and down. When held in portrait mode, the entire height of the image can be seen and there is actually no tilt function. Even so, in both modes, the camera image is squeezed together and not at the correct aspect ratio (I guess this depends on your phone's aspect ratio because the programmers chose not to maintain aspect ratio of the picture).

The recording function is fairly basic. It works like a dashcam in that the camera is always recording and will loop back over itself once the storage is filled.

As with any other wifi home automation product, a separate account needs to be created to log in to the app -- an app one must trust to not send any sensitive information back to the mothership. Personally, I plug this camera into a smart switch that I can turn on only when I'm out so that at least the camera isn't on when I'm at home.

So this camera will do what it advertises but it there really isn't anything that sets it apart from the large number of products out there. Wyze, while being a little bit bigger, costs only $30 and has actual tilt function.

I understand that the Type-C standard is tricky sometimes. Type-C chargers need to agree with the device on the correct voltage to use and the amperage of the charger must be enough to drive the device for power to actually be delivered successfully.

With that said, I purchased the F1TP DMW-DCC8 USB-C Power Adapter DC Coupler Set for my Panasonic Lumix GX-8. I tried this adapter on every Type-C charger I have, a cell phone charger, a powerbank, and one that's rated for the Nintendo Switch (enough for the console to switch to TV mode). None of them got the slightest reaction from this adapter.

I really wanted the flexibility of the Type-C connection for my Lumix camera, especially if I wanted to use is as a webcam through an HDMI capture card, but this one just didn't work out.

I own the original Osmo Pocket and it can be controlled by WIFI through an adapter. With this clip, the camera can be clipped to a backpack to record a "first person view" type of video. It can then be monitored from a smart phone. With the built in gimbal, the video will be very smooth except for the "gimbal bob" (up and down movement when walking normal) that's unavoidable with this device. It frees up your hands while still capturing the video.

It is unfortunate that this device has pretty bad build quality. The included GoPro style screw adapter wasn't able to reach the hex nut. In trying to force the screw in, I stripped part of it. I had other gopro adapters lying around so I was able to find a replacement. Even when screwed in, the fit isn't very tight. The joint is loose and will move when walking around. There just isn't enough friction between the parts to make it stay where you set it.

Placing a camera around the house, one faces the problem of how to provide power to the device. Traditional systems used BNC coaxial connectors but as video resolutions increased, POE (Power-Over-Ethernet) systems became popular. Both types of systems required pulling wires around the house. POE is still the best solution because they are secure and won't hog up your wifi bandwidth due to being wired.

When only one or two cameras are needed, wifi cameras (preferably solar powered ones) provide a great solution to the problem. This wireless solar camera has many good qualities going for it. It is compact, and completely self-contained. While it can be charged via USB, the built-in solar panel will do a good job charging the internal battery throughout the day.

It has night vision, but no infrared LED's to help light the scene. Still, the nightvision does a good job all by itself. Motion sensor is built in and will send alerts to the app. One great feature is that there is no monthly subscription necessary to get recordings due to its built-in microsd card slot. The app allows one to highlight a section of the recording to save to the phone. Combine all of this with its relatively low price, this is a very attractive security camera!

So what are the drawbacks? The overall execution of the camera is somewhat disappointing. There is a huge problem consumers are facing when it comes to building a smart home. One either has to:
1. Pay an exorbitant amount of money for branded devices that connects back to a company that one hopes is trustworthy and still be required to purchase a monthly plan to get all the features.
2. Spend less money on unknown brands, but have to deal with each device requiring a different app to operate, but more disturbingly, trusting ones home security to an unknown entity outside of ones country.

This camera relies on the Tuya or Smart Life app to operate. This app has really become the defacto standard for all low-cost or unbranded smart home devices. The company behind the app is based in China so please make your own decision regarding whether this is safe for you. The devices live on your wifi network and connects back to its home server and the app lives in your phone with requirements to access your storage and GPS location, also requiring a login that connects back to its home server.

Security concerns aside, there are three issues with the recording functionality of the camera. Firstly, the microsd slot only accepts cards up to 32gb. At 1080p quality, this means perhaps 240min of video storage. This leads to a potential issue which is the second point: the recording function is similar to a dash cam in that it is always recording. Video is recorded in a loop and old footage is overwritten when the card is filled. The constant writes to a microsd, of course shortens its lifespan, but even more importanly, a better execution would have been to take advantage of the motion sensor and cache 60 seconds of video in memory and write to the card when motion is detected. The last point regarding the recording function is that if the camera is turned off while the SD card is in the slot, it will NOT be detected when the device is turned back on. One must eject the card and reinsert it (while the camera is on) for recording to start again. Combine this with the overpowered spring in the SD Card slot and you'll be guaranteed to lose your memory card because if you do not insert the card successfully on the first try, it will be ejected a few feet away and you will spend your time looking through your bushes trying to find it again.

Please listen to the other reviewers for this product when they tell you that this device is a fire hazard. With their warnings in mind, I took the chance and plugged it into my computer. Within 10 seconds, the onboard chip became too hot to touch. I immediately removed it and won't risk trying to flash anything with it.

Please be careful.

Edit: just over one month in, the right earbud stopped working.

There are many, many true wireless earbuds out there. What attracted me to these were the features that they boasted: Wireless Charging, Active Noise-Cancelling, and bluetooth 5.1. So how does these earbuds compare to some of the cheaper offerings and does it justify being twice as expensive as some of them?

In terms of price, these earbuds can be considered cheap. Comparable to the mid-tier brands out there such as Anker and MPow, and much, much cheaper than Bose and Jabra brands. Still, there are many that cost half the price.

With the pricing in mind, let's look at the good of these earbuds:
+ Long battery life -- I'm on my fourth hour of listening to an audiobook and the battery is still showing 50% on my phone.
+ Battery status reporting to phone -- I'm sure most of the recent bluetooth headphones and earbuds do this now, but it is still nice.
+ Type-C port for charging -- The move to type-c as the standard charging port for all devices is happening and I'm glad NANNIO didn't cheap out and use a micro-usb. One less cable to worry about.
+ No app necessary -- The passthrough and ANC features can be turned on by tapping the touch controls twice.
+ Google Assistant Support -- Tap three times and Google Assistant launches.
+ No ugly microphone stick -- The tear-drop shape of these buds look much better than the ugly sticks that Apple's products have, in my opinion.
+ Smooth transition between left-only, right-only, and stereo -- These earbuds allow one to choose to use only one earbud while keeping the other in the charger without having to pair the other piece separately. It's something that I take advantage of on long drives. I keep one bud in the ear to listen to my audiobook and switch out when the battery runs out.

The bad:
- Not low profile -- The Anker SoundCores is pretty inconspicuous in the ear, but these NANNIOs, being white and sticking out more are anything but low profile.
- ANC not very effective -- The ANC levels are adjusted to be pretty minimal on these buds so while it is possible to hear the difference between the feature being on and off, it is also noticeable that only the lowest hums are cancelled out. Earbuds simply aren't good for ANC. Buds simply don't fit perfectly in the ear canal and when the jaw moves, the fit shifts. By this fact, there is always sound leaking through, reducing the efficiency of any ANC system. In earbuds, ANC is really just a gimmick.
- Passthrough needs to have wind noise reduction -- The reason for passthrough, in my mind, is to be able to hear surrounding sounds if wearing earbuds while running. It uses the microphone on the earbuds to pass external sounds through, but when running, there will always be wind noise. Without wind noise reduction, it makes this feature useless. I don't know of any earbuds that have addressed this issue.

So why did I still give these buds 5-stars? Because it is priced perfectly for what it is and what it promises. It has more features and quality that makes it better than the lower $30 dollar earbuds, but isn't a brand that can demand over $100. The features that are promised are delivered and any shortcomings are expected, as described above. With these buds, I get

While this dolly is useful for rotating the camera around an object, I also saw this product as an option for cases where I did not wish to bring the slider track with me. I'd be able to have the dolly on a ledge and get panning shots for b-rolls.

Unfortunately, a couple of things made it a bad fit for me:
-- Difficult to place object in the center. Being that the dolly is not on track, it was difficult to get the dolly to rotate around the subject. When I placed the dolly far enough away from the subject to fit it all in the frame, I found that the subject would eventually become off-center or go completely off frame because it wasn't perfectly in the center. I ended up having to tighten the turning radius and place the camera fairly close to the subject to shoot a complete 360 pan successfully. This would be the same complaint I'd have about any other dolly that's not on a track, I would imagine.

-- Lowest speed too slow for the timelapse I wanted. I have a plant whose leaves close at sun down and open again at dawn. I wanted to get a timelapse of this while the camera did a 360 pan. I estimated the leaves to close over a period of 3 hours so I set up my timelapse. The end result was that the dolly ran out of battery power at around 2 hours and 30 minutes and the resulting video was one where the plant moved slowly but the camera panned too quickly.

-- Tricky balance. Being three-wheeled, it was a little tricky to balance the dolly with my mirrorless camera. It actually tipped over while I was trying to set it up, dilocating part of the lens. Fortunately, I was able to pop the lens back together without any real damage.

There are so many good things about GripGear's Movie Maker 2 Set that I just had to take the plunge and purchase it despite some of the problems identified by various youtube reviews. Unfortunately, I have to agree with many of their points and eventually, had to admit that some are showstoppers for me.

First, I want to state what is good about the Movie Maker 2 Set:
-- Low cost, comparatively. While there are other sliders that are in the same price range, those don't have the same versatility and portability. The motor can be used by itself to get 360 panorama shots and the track can be broken down and easily fit in a backpack. Additional lengths of track can also be purchased separately at a low cost. No other product on Amazon does all of this and would require separate purchases.
-- Remote control. While we expect remotes for almost everything electronics these days, I was surprised by the fact that many sliders/panorama motors do not come with one.
-- Versatility. Already mentioned previously, but I really want to emphasize that this is a unique feature of this product. In addition to the points already listed, the Movie Maker 2 set can also be used vertically

Negatives:
-- Top speed too slow: I'm in agreement with many youtube reviews that the highest speed is still not fast enough for some shots. This is why you will see many videos shot with this movie maker set sped up, making all of the videos look like timelapses.
-- Lowest speed too fast: When doing actual timelapse over two or three hours, the resulting video pans too fast. So while your timelapse subject is moving at the right speed, the camera movement is just too fast, making it uncomfortable to watch.

-- Weak 1/4" camera mount. The motor is made very specifically for the camera mount that was included with the set. Unfortunately, if your camera is not balanced or front heavy, it is difficult to get the tilt head to stay put without some grunt work turning the tightening screw.

I'm not a professional cinematographer so I thought my requirements would not be very strict, but not being able to get the shots I wanted due to the speed limitations makes me feel like this set is ALMOST what I wanted but it's just not there yet. I hope that the manufacturer can improve this product a little more and bring it across the finish line.
After a week or so some of the frequently used keys became very wobbly. I cleaned my original OEM keyboard, reinstalled it, and threw this thing out.

I know nothing about vinyl players so I got this one because it seems like a great beginner player. We recently moved in to a new house and needed this mount to install a TV on our patio. I measured the VESA holes on our TV and knew this would work prior to ordering so that was not an issue.

This will hold a 55” Visio TV from a vaulted ceiling.

Installation is not as straightforward as I have experienced with other mounts though not terribly difficult either. The issues with installation really come from limited space to work to attach the parts together and there not being great instructions.

A few tips we found as we installed that will help you - first locate your ceiling joist stud to mount into. Then find the distance from the wall where your TV can swivel both left and right to the farthest point you desire - then mark your spot.

As with all mounting brackets you want to mount into a stud with as many bolts as possible.

In terms of use this works but there are features that just should be more user friendly. For instance if the height is in the highest position the cables will be pinched in place and can not be moved at all - the cable pass through should have a notch so this is not an issue as it is never good to have cables being pinched.

In addition if you want to either swivel or tilt the TV a hex key is required instead of being able to do this with a finger tightening knob like most mounts - this is definitely the worst design flaw in my opinion. This issue has left us unable to rotate our TVs mount that is “able to swivel” when we’ve had guests at our house due to not being able to locate the correct sized hex key. Ugh.

This mount works, but I would really only recommend it for locations where the user does not intend to alter the tilt or direction of the TVs screen very often.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

If you are new to home security camera systems, I recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with POE cameras run off of quality POE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. One disadvantage of higher megapixel cameras is the recordings will take up more hard drive space. Depending on the number of cameras, this can become a larger concern.

When I saw this camera at this price point I knew it was something I needed to check out. I appreciated the fact it was 2MP because with this lens you are not going to want to be eating up the hard drive space required for a 5MP.

I was able to get it set up within my Blue Iris system after playing with it for a while. Typically this takes me no more than a couple of minutes - this camera required much more extensive programming in order to have it functional.

Once I did have it up and working image quality is substandard even compared to other cameras with similar specs.

I figured it still could be utilized as a tertiary filler camera but it kept going offline for absolutely no reason. When a camera is connected via PoE to Blue Iris this simply should not be an issue unless there are issues with the camera itself.

While the price point is excellent on this camera, unfortunately this is an example of getting what you pay for. In my four months of testing this camera has proven to be unreliable, difficult to connect and keep connected and the images captured are far lower quality than expected from cameras with similar specs.

This is a product to pass on.

It will work fine for iPhones or smaller tablets but if you intend on using this for an iPad Pro you will want to replace at least one of the manufacturer’s springs with a 7/16” x 1-1/2” extension spring. Here is what I used - https://www.amazon.com/dp/B008RFNRIW/ref=cm_sw_em_r_mt_dp_Pq.TFbC339YC7

After replacing the spring I had no further issues and the floor stand operates as it should. This would be an easy correction for the manufacturer to make but currently as it is delivered I would not recommend this item for users of the iPad Pro. While the fix is not difficult, when purchasing a product marketed specifically for that unit we should not have to modify the product in any way.

If the correct springs were included this would be a solid 5 star item, as it is I give it a 3 and advise ordering the spring when purchasing the stand if you want to use this with your Pro.

Security Warning: All devices from Xiongmai, a Chinese OEM who manufactures white-label video surveillance equipment, come with an always-on cloud feature called XMEye P2P cloud. This feature contains serious vulnerabilities that allow attacks on millions of devices, even ones that are behind firewalls.

Millions of security cameras, DVRs, and NVRs contain vulnerabilities that can allow a remote attacker to take over devices with little effort, security researchers have revealed recently.

All vulnerable devices have been manufactured by Hangzhou Xiongmai Technology Co., Ltd. (often referred to as Xiongmai), a Chinese company based in the city of Hangzhou.

End users won't be able to tell that they're using a hackable device because the company doesn't sell any products with its name on them, but ships all equipment as white label products on which other companies put their logo on top. Evtevision is one of said companies.

If the product description mentions anything about "XMEye," then despite the logo on the front of the device, the equipment was made by Xiongmai.

As you can see in the third bulleted point at the top of the listing:

“Easy view on Smartphone via Xmeye, PC tablet via CMS,and Web browser IE.”

This is, without question, a Xiongmai device. Installing it or any of its software would place the privacy and security of you and your family in serious jeopardy.

Most security companies have banned selling these types of cameras for the reasons I have explained.

As soon as I opened this camera and started examining it I recognized some telltale signs and therefore did not set this up on my network. I caution everyone to avoid these products completely.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

As with all security systems my advice is never use cloud based recording - this opens your entire network to not only the company who you are giving blanket access too but also to hackers. The same is true for WiFi. Obviously WiFi is more convenient but if your privacy is a concern this really needs to be taken into account. Hackers have become quite adept at hacking into WiFi cameras and being able to not only watch your feed but control your cameras and access your entire network. If you choose to utilize WiFi cameras take the time to understand your router and employ proper VPN protocols.

In terms of this particular wireless WiFi camera by MYPIN it can accept up to a 128GB TF card. While this would provide plenty of space to record if only set to motion unless you subscribe it will only save the previous 7 days worth of data. This is ludicrous - this is the company manipulating users into having to subscribe.

The built in camera and apps on the iPhone allow for so much more creative work than most of us lovers of photography ever dreamed possible - there is no reason not to enjoy that technology. Years ago I never would have dreamed of shooting photos with my phone rather than my DSLR but that is, in fact, often the case.

This has led me to testing, evaluating and reviewing many accessories that make creative shooting with the phone even more versatile than it is natively.

I’ve reviewed a few similar lens kits. This one comes with macro, wide angle and zoom lenses, a mini tripod for the zoom lens, the adapters needed to attach the lenses to the phone and a case for it all.

The wide angle and macro lenses are both decent quality - not professional quality but adequate for hobby enthusiasts. Of the three lenses the macro is the best. The wide angle causes photos focus to get soft towards the edges.

Unfortunately the zoom lens is sub par. While I can get it to work images are consistently below average. Zoom lenses work by utilizing a series of lenses that must be perfectly aligned to capture an accurate, crisp image. While I use excellent photography apps on my iPhone X and worked adjusting the zoom lens I never could get photos near as crisp as with other sets.

This is a mediocre set - I’ve reviewed much worse and a few better, although they were at higher price points. At this price point this is not a bad deal but I certainly wouldn’t rave about this set.

Being both an audiophile and a lover of all new tech when I first read about this technology coming out a few years ago I started looking forward to testing it.

So what are the potential advantages of bone conduction earphones? I’m glad you asked. When properly adjusted they allow the user to enjoy listening to whatever they choose while not blocking external noises, thus allowing the user to react to ambient noises. This should make them safe to use while driving or doing other activities that require hearing ambient noise in order to conduct safely.

Unfortunately these R9 headphones allow for very little fine adjustment. In order for this type of headphones to work properly and provide the highest sound quality they should rest flat, or almost flat against the skin between the front of the ear and the rear part of the cheek bone. When adjusting the speaker it is clear when the speaker is properly adjusted. The adjustment that I was able to do came from working the rubber casing and sliding the speaker further onto the arm that wraps around the back of the head. By twisting the speaker inward I was able to get the speaker closer to the proper location but not exactly correct. Due to this, sound quality is not optimal and surrounding people are able to hear what the listener is playing.

In terms of design choices I find it odd that while it’s estimated between 70-95% of the population of any ethnicity is right handed this manufacturer chose to place the controls on the left side. This makes controlling them both awkward and difficult. While the buttons operate in a standard press and double press pattern it is awkward reaching across and doing it on the left side.

In terms of operation these headphones maintain a solid connection for the full 33 feet they are rated for and the batteries lasted approximately 6.25 hours on the first full charge cycle. Sound quality is middle of the road especially due to not allowing for fine adjusting of the speakers.

With a couple of minor changes these headphones would be a much better product. If the speakers are held in the correct positions it is much better - if an adjustment system were added these could potentially have much higher sound quality. In addition, obviously the controls should be placed on the right side for ease and regularity of access.

This is a great technology with a lot of potential. These headphones while not capable of fine adjustments would probably fit someone with an average sized head better. My head is a bit smaller than average which made these fit a bit too large for me.

I had high hopes for this docking station from StarTech but, thus far, I’ve been pretty disappointed.

Like many people I like the portability of working from a laptop but when I am at my workstation I want more screen space to work on - I thought this Docking Station would be a perfect solution. Well, in theory, it would.

Inside the box you’ll find the docking station, a 3.0 USB cable, a power adapter with snap on plugs to fit various world power sources, a DVI to VGA adapter, and a CD-ROM.

Unlike many docking stations or hubs this is not Plug and Play. I’m running the most updated Windows 10 64bit and the CD-ROM is completely useless. After inserting it in my computer I received a message reading that it was not compatible with my machine. No problem, I went to the manufacturer’s website, found the product, clicked on support, downloaded the zip file containing the setup and updated drivers for my OS and continued.

I went through the installation process and it appeared to install fine. After accepting the user agreement it checked my system for compatibility - finding no issues it continued and completed installation. I went to device manager and noticed an error in USB connected devices but figured with a restart it would correct.

I restarted but the error remains. Configuration Descriptor Request Failed - Windows has stopped device. I have uninstalled and reinstalled, searched help, used Windows Update to search for a better driver - so far nothing has worked.

In regards to functionality - the USB ports (two 3.0 and four 2.0) all function without issue and the Ethernet Port works great providing me over 200Mb/s. Due to not having the correct drivers I’ve been unable to test the multiple monitor capabilities.

I have contacted tech support and as of writing I have not heard back. If they are able to help me solve these issues I will update my review to reflect my further findings.

It appears this Docking Station is outdated being developed for older operating systems and while it may work for some users, others will find it needlessly difficult.

I would look at more recently manufactured docking stations that have been developed with the current operating systems - especially if you are using Windows 10.

The biggest difference between this projector & the much more expensive projectors in professional settings is the bulb. This one does a fine job in low light or with back light but will completely wash out with light around or over the screen. I ordered this primarily to do presentations & show videos at my club meetings. It performed well but we did have to fiddle a bit with the lights in the room & the position of the projector.

The usefulness of this projector is its portability & low cost. It is lightweight & compact & fairly easy to set up. I would have appreciated a padded carry case for the projector but the box it comes in works pretty well. It has foam that surrounds the projector, it holds all the cords, it has a handle & it is easily sturdy enough to set the projector on for more height.

It helps a lot with the focus & clarity if the projector is nearly horizontal. That means that if the projection screen is to be 4' over the ground then the projector also needs to be 4' off the ground which is generally going to be much higher than a table. The focus ring around the lens works very well to dial in the clarity. There is a foot that unscrews from the bottom front to angle the projector up. I tried propping something under the front to angle it higher but the image distorts & loses clarity the more it is tilted.

The biggest issue I have had with the projector is the image source. I can't get either of my laptop computers to recognize the projector as an external screen with the HDMI cable but the HDMI works on a DVD player. The IOS control works pretty well with my iPad. My Pixel phone doesn't support the built-in Miracast. The Bluetooth only recognizes my Samsung TV & none of my phones, computers or tablets sees the projector's Bluetooth signal. It has a YouTube app built into the device software but it is un-useable due to a cumbersome search process that doesn't return any results. I ended up using it with a USB thumb drive which works well & the menu is easy enough to navigate but takes some learning. I did not try the AV cable inputs or the SD memory slot.

This actually fits my needs pretty well, I just wanted a BT speaker for my daughter to use to practice her routines instead of turning the speakers all the way up on her iPhone. The sound is generated by a single-cone speaker, about 4" diameter & the enclosure doesn't do much to improve the sound. It probably won't sound as good as the device it's hooked to but it is louder & without distortion.
Bluetooth setup is easy but it will only link to one device at a time, I have to "forget" it from another device before linking to another. I haven't used it with USB, or micro SD (or even the audio jack) but since it doesn't have any kind of display I think it would be a pain to play anything but a pre-arranged set list or track albums. I have never run the battery all the way down so I don't know how long it lasts but it lasts a while.

They are very comfortable, stay in the ear very well & I like that they grip the inner ear instead of going around the ear. Only having the inner ear clamps also makes the charger smaller. The earbuds charge in a small box that has a battery of it's own so they can recharge in a pocket.

It's hard to hate on this drone when it is flying. Mechanically it performs very well in the air. The camera is great & the camera stabilization works very well. The app has been a frustrating experience that has kept me from fully exploring the capabilities of the drone.

After the last app & firmware update we have experienced freezing of the video feed, disconnects from the phone & disconnects from the radio. The good news is that, in the last case, the drone dutifully returned to its starting spot. I didn't have those issues before the update but I did have others.

I have put in a couple of tech requests & their support is very good. In some cases a confirmation email the same or next day & resolution in another day or so. In one case a very nice young man called me to talk me through a gyro calibration.

We have enjoyed using the camera to fly it around the neighborhood. The camera function is fantastic. The attitude adjustment for the camera is intuitive & handy. I'm still learning to fly by the screen so I like being able to "look" up & down to make sure I'm not about to hit something and figure out the location by looking at landmarks & streets.

On the drone platform, the camera can be set to track a person with just the camera & the drone stationary or have the drone follow the person while tracking. We used that to record my daughter's color guard practice. It also has a "point of interest" feature where it flies circles over a particular spot & the operator can start or stop recording while it it is circling. I'm thinking this will be cool for parties this Summer when we can finally have people over again. For now I have is top quality shots of the top of my camper & green pool.

It camera mode it performs very well as a stable, tracking camera. The camera gimble has a lot of range to track a person moving about & the tracking works well. If the person moves out of the frame it will not re-aquire them though in my experience. The camera can be mounted on a tripod or used as a hand-held "camcorder". On a tripod, it kind of hangs off to the side & down so it will interfere with some tripod setups. It is also a bit bulky to use as a camcorder but the stabilization is so good I forgive that. In either configuration a phone has to be used to stop & start recording or take pictures which I do not like & I hope they put out a bluetooth button for that.

The controller is small compared to the ones I used for model airplanes & it is easy to hold. There is no attachment point for a lanyard. The phone is held on a mount that extends out & up & puts the phone in a good place to see but puts a lot of weight up high. The gimbles have a rubber gasket around that makes them water resistant & doesn't interfere with their operation. The controller charges with a mini-usb (ugh) & connects to the phone with included USBC or Lightning cables. The cord going to the phone could be a little more tidy.

The case is nice, thick foam & will hold everything needed to fly except maybe a second battery. It's sturdy enough to put in checked luggage (with the batteries removed of course).

The beginner mode is seriously slow & a good way to get used to flying especially for someone who is learning nose-in hovering & other basics. It also makes a very stable camera platform.

A couple of observations:
I am not great at sorting out things on the app & would prefer robust instructions. I had no idea that the aforementioned gyro calibration was something I could perform myself or that I should have known where to look for it. It took me several tries to figure out how to turn on the tracking features (it has to be "started" after turning it on).

This is my first serious drone so I can't adequately compare it to other models. I used to fly model airplanes & helicopters decades ago & I tend to try to fly these quadrotors like an airplane in line of sight flight. This model seems to resist that more than others that I have flown & tries to force a flat plane rather than let me bank it & swoop around (I hope that makes sense).

I worked in a hobby shop for several years when I was younger (a long time ago). This is exactly what people who came in dreamed of buying; a small, aircraft that could fly in the backyard or far away that doesn't require a steep learning curve to fly or maintain. The camera adds to the fun & makes it useful.

When this thing is working it works but I have to completely reset it from time to time since I got it three months ago.  I don't use many devices on this network but I use it as a repeater to a third router in a detached building which makes it extra painful to reset.  Talk about your first world problems.

but the major problem is the whole in the eye piece that your phone camera lens looks through covers only part of the lens no matter how much you try to center it. The corner fasteners are plastic corners rather than elastic binders. I don't know exactly how snug the tablet would fit (I have a Galaxy Note 10.1 rather than a Tab Pro) My Note tablet does not fit, which I thought it would because they are both supposed to be the same size.

The whole case feels cheap, and there is very little cushioning. The tri-fold does work well to prop up the tablet, but if you were to accidentally drop your tablet in this case, I feel sure it would fall out. I don't have much confidence that it would protect the tablet very well at all.

[[VIDEOID:d9cb51d1c95a2bc172f8fec24c5f713b]] As you can see in the video, the keyboard is very cute, even though you need to sort of remove it and pull forward to get the tablet to stand. But the real problem is, even after I started getting used to the smaller keys, I noticed the equal key (=) started acting up. Sometimes it would get stuck on by itself, just pressing the key repeatedly. Other times it would refuse to fire at all. This is after using it for less than one day.
Considering that the keyboard in my case is used because I want to type in exact syntax commands (something an on screen keyboard is bad at), having functional number keys and an equal sign is important. I sadly can't recommend that keyboard for this reason.
