[[VIDEOID:3d513e57441130c25fa7c0b6059a91ae]] I really like this concept. It's tiny, and projects an image onto a surface that looks a lot better than I expected. I own some professional grade projectors that I use for work, so to be fair, you can't compare it to a real product like that. For starters, this needs an extremely dark room to work in. Don't even bother during daylight hours unless you have a room with no windows.
But, it comes with Android built in so you're actually able to stream content without plugging anything into it! You can install standard streaming apps, or load up an SD card with content to play, or use the ports behind the rubber gasket if necessary. This thing even does auto keystone if you tilt it, which really surprised and impressed me! And because the back is flat and doesn't block any vents, you can actually lie it down facing the ceiling!
But here's the fatal flaw: The battery isn't great, and when it dies it is very easy to get stuck in this sort of "limbo" state. I managed to twice already boot it without enough battery left to finish booting, and it gets stuck in this trying-to-turn-on mode in which it won't turn off but also won't turn on. Sometimes you can get the projector to show the boot logo if there's enough power for that, but then if it doesn't finish, it shuts off and gets stuck. You can see a little blue light inside, hear something making noise if you hold it to your ear, but it won't finish booting. It also won't TURN OFF. It's stuck like that, the power switch position doesn't matter once this happens. And charging it up won't help either. You need to wait for the battery to totally die (you can see the blue light inside finally turn off) and THEN charge it all the way up, and then it will boot and work correctly.
This is a pretty big flaw in my opinion. This thing really could have used a reset button or way to pull the battery in case this happens. The instructions are pretty terrible too, most of it I had to figure out on my own. But if they can manage to fix that flaw, this is an impressively cool device! I'm going to try and keep it charged and use it on our next camping trip, I really love that you can sit it on it's back and aim the projector at a ceiling! But part of me feels like it is pretty likely to get stuck in this state again.

I like how much you can fit into this bag, it's got a uniform box shape instead of the classic tapered backpack (narrow at the top and wider at the bottom). The advantage to this is that it can fit more things inside while still fitting into the guidelines for under-seat storage on a flight. The downside is that it doesn't look as nice when worn- this is a function over form design.
That's fine- the problem for me, however, is that this bag lacks the rigidity I was expecting to protect the contents inside. In fact, the bag actually ships folded over on itself, that's how flexible the material is. I'm used to there being more of a backing to protect, say, a laptop in the rear pocket. As it is now, the laptop is what holds the bag's shape. I actually think I'd rather stick to my older backpack which was more stylish and protective when I travel, but this will come in handy when I need to fit more things in carry on.

Sadly, the point-and-shoot camera market has been cannibalized by phones, so you can't really find simple cameras like this from big brands anymore. Real point and shoot cameras were great because unlike phones, you get a zoom lens and real camera controls. This isn't that.
Additionally, this is NOT going to compete with a modern cell phone camera. It's about on par with a low end entry level cell phone, the kind that you can usually get for free with a contract (maybe barely a mid range and DEFINITELY not a flagship). It does NOT zoom, there is a digital zoom only. The good news is that it comes with a decent sized memory card and two batteries, so you can have a spare one ready to go. I wish it came with a battery charger so you can keep one on tap (the only way to charge the battery is IN the camera, which means you can't charge one while using the other sadly), but the fact you get a backup is nice at least.
The pictures aren't great, but they're fun for a kid to run around with. I can see an elementary school aged kid having fun with this, my 5 and 10 year old like it well enough. The item suggests "4-15 year old" and to be honest, I can NOT see a 15 year old enjoying this AT ALL. My 12 year old has a similar camera that is waterproof so at least she can say it's fun to use in the pool (which she does), but this kind of underwhelmed me for the asking price.

[[VIDEOID:d7dac93a9ae5119758136812fcd18f71]] I'm very familiar with Atoto as a brand, I've used 3 of their aftermarket radios on different vehicles previously so I was excited to try this one.

I'll go into a full blown review in a moment, but first let me point out the problem no one seems to be talking about:
This is great and really easy to use (wireless Android Auto even automatically starts on power up) ...as long as you are the only driver of the car. You see, the Bluetooth system can pair with multiple phones, but it will only look for the last one you used when it boots up. Share the car with a family member? You'll have to go into the bluetooth menu and find the list of paired phones, click on yours and THEN it will connect and work properly, and it will continue to do so automatically whenever you get back into the car, as expected. But when that family member drives again? They'll have to do the same thing for their phone, taking the auto-connect away from yours! It's very very frustrating if you have multiple drivers on a family vehicle.
Atoto has similar functionality on their Android powered A6 and S8 units, however not their F7 (linux powered). They told me it has to do with the way Android security works, however this unit does not run Android natively so I assumed it would be like the F7. Sadly not. I can't recommend this unit to families or multiple users of a vehicle for that reason.

Otherwise, if you're the lone driver of your car, and you have an older car that lacks Android Auto (or even Bluetooth), this is DEFINITELY worth looking into. It offers Bluetooth for calls and music streaming as well as full blown Android Auto to mirror your apps to the display (both wired and wirelessly), yet requires no modification to your dash.

The concept is a good one, I know plenty of people who would love these features but don't want to replace their OEM radio. And for the most part, it works well- I like the way it is a single harness and one cable going down to the DC port, your aux/USB/etc all plugs down there. Similar units from other brands I've seen had all ports on the screen unit, so everything (USB port, aux, power, etc) was yet another wire going up to the dash top and looking like a spidery-mess. Hiding one wire is much more manageable. And you have the options of using aux out, FM out, or just using the unit's own loudspeaker.
I really hope Atoto will realize they need the bluetooth system to look for other paired phones when the last one used doesn't connect. OEM factory bluetooth systems work like that for a reason, and there is no security excuse here.

I want to start off saying this thing has INCREDIBLE potential. For the same price as a mini PC, you can get a fully fledged tablet running a desktop version of Windows! Not only that, but the build quality seems pretty incredible for a cheap tablet, the back of it is actually a rubberized material that keeps it free of fingerprints and slipping out of your hands... it doesn't need a case, in other words. I haven't used a tablet that I felt didn't need a case in years!
It has limited storage, but that's expected of a cheap computing machine. It does have an expandable slot for additional storage, and the 4GB of ram is enough for most basic computing. You're not going to be using this for high end gaming, but you can plow through most desktop and office applications as well as browsing and streaming without a hiccup. The things that bothered me, however are:
a) It has USB-C, but does not allow itself to be charged with it. Unlike modern tablets and laptops that use PD chargers to juice up over the USBC, this actually uses a tiny proprietary plug that is almost certainly going to get lost eventually. It's not like it will be easy to find replacements or backups unlike major brands like HP and Lenovo, if I ever lose this plug I'm probably out of luck. I don't understand why it couldn't have used PD over the USB-c like every other modern device.
b) This one is a little bit more serious, but it complains that Windows is not activated. If you try to activate it, you are told that the server won't allow activation and to contact the vendor. I'm not entirely sure how to do that, and instead I'm left with a suspiciously inactivated version of Windows. Feels almost like for this price the software isn't licensed, which concerns me. I'm going to try and found out what it will take to activate, but it is definitely something you should know before plunking down money on a tablet that might not be using legitimate software.
Otherwise it is pretty useful for the price.

I bought this to use in my minivan's A6 pf to send the video out to the rear seats. The plan was to be able to stream content throughout the car.
At first it did not seem to be doing anything, there is a glowing red LED so I know it's connected but nothing appeared on the external screen. At some point during testing I saw what appears to be a casting icon on the top of the display and the screen was mirroring, but I have been unable to get that to happen again. I tried resetting, changing USB ports, changing monitors to a portable RCA input screen I have... I even tried it on my other car which has an Atoto S8 ultra (gen 2). Both of these radios are listed as compatible yet nothing worked. I don't know if I just got a lemon but this has not at all been working. It comes with no instructions so there isn't even any troubleshooting guide to follow.

I could not get this to to work.
I use AV equipment for a living, and sometimes I need to convert an HDMI signal to an analog RCA one. In the past I've had to use an adapter (box powered by 5v) to achieve that. I was hoping this was somehow a streamlined version of that which is self powered or something (I know HDMI ports have some residual power), but that doesn't seem to be the case.
I see on the description here that it "can't be directly transferred from PC, laptop, DVD, PS4, xbox and other devices with HDMI interface to TV." So then what DOES it work for?
I tried connecting several types of devices to the RCA input of a TV and nothing seems to work. I tried a Firestick, a camera, an Android box, Raspberry Pi, mini PC, etc. Nothing.

I'm scratching my head trying to understand what on earth this could be used for. I think I'd recommend a traditional HDMI digital to analog RCA converter box if you're trying to go from one to the other.

Ok, to be fair I work with cameras for a living. I wasn't expecting this to compete with my cinema cameras or even popular DSLRs for video, but I was expecting it to at least hold up to the standards people are expecting from cell phone cameras these days. It doesn't. Aside from filling a 4K frame, there aren't a lot of positives to say about the video quality.
To be fair, this has a LOT of advantages over using a cell phone. Recording for long lengths of time onto an SD card is a big plus, not the mention the ability to mount it to a standard tripod and have accessories like a mic and light attached to the body (which are all included!). It comes with a wide angle lens (that is oddly called "macro", but no- it's not for macro shots, its for going wider) which screws on to the front, as well as a handle mounting bracket, an LED light and a microphone. It even comes with a 64GB card, a spare battery, and not one but TWO useful carrying cases (a large one for everything, and a smaller one for just the camera solo). But that's about all the positives I can say about it. If you are outside with a lot of light, you can get decent shots, but this isn't a zoom lens, the zoom is digital only. You can go wide with the external lens or just stay at a fixed medium without it. So no closeup shots for soccer moms. The dynamic range when using it indoors was pretty bad, worse than your average mid-range cell phone. Forget about low light. But that's ok, because the ergonomics of a camera make it better than a cell phone, right?
Well, sorta. Holding it with the strap and the flip out screen is nice. But the UI is confusing, it's hard to go back and watch clips you took because everything is kind of sluggish and not intuitive- once we went past the first page of recorded clips, it was really difficult to move to the next page without accidentally clicking and opening a clip for playback. It just feels really laggy to navigate. Then there's the mic input... it's actually a proprietary plug that goes into the charging/USB plug, and gives you a pigtail for USB on one side and a mic input jack on the other. Odd, considering it COMES with a mic, you'd think it would have an input directly on the body. But no, just this weird mess of wires. Everything about this feels like jumping through a hoop to make it do what you want, and at the end of the day you have to wonder if you couldn't just be better off getting a mic adapter for the cellphone you already own and putting it in one of those holster cages.
Speaking of cell phones, this does have an app which supposedly lets you remotely control and perhaps even copy files from it, but I didn't get that far. I tried to install the app but then gave up when I decided I didn't want to grant this all the permissions it wanted from my personal phone. And I didn't think the video quality was worth it either.
Oddly enough, I kind of like the accessories it comes with. The LED light is pretty nice, the mic isn't terrible either. But for the money, I feel like I would have rather skipped those accessories and just gotten a better camera for a little bit more. It feels almost like they realized this camera was a hard sell so they beefed it up with lots of a accessories for the price.
In conclusion, you DO get a lot of accessories for the money. It's not the worst camera I've ever used, and you can't really get a set with everything you need for any less so I'd say it's worth at least 3 stars for being a functional kit. But I can't really imagine a scenario that I would recommend it.

This is a great player for those of us with older DVDs that we want to play on a modern (or older, it does have RCA plugs!) TV. It works, and the TV displayed the upscaled image just fine, however the remote almost killed the experience.
For starters, the batteries it came with were physically warped, but no big deal- I don't usually expect batteries to be included, so I tossed them away and put fresh ones in. But then the remote did not seem to work. Fine, I'll just use the controls on the player, right? WRONG. The only option on the player is the play/pause button. So if your DVD has a menu that starts with the cursor over play, that's fine. But if you need to navigate the menus at all, you're out of luck without the remote working. There is no D-pad or any other obvious way to get the cursor to move.
But then I thankfully read another review here that described not getting the remote to work unless it was in direct line-of-sight with the TOP of the player (as if mounted to a wall in the picture- basically it isn't just that it CAN be wall mounted, it is designed to ONLY work properly in that angle!). Well folks, it does work if only in that exact scenario, which is kind of boggling. If this gets used in a classroom or senior center, the experience will not be intuitive without being told you have to hold the remote in a very specific orientation for it to work. I've never seen an IR remote that was so picky... usually if you point a remote at something nearby the sensor, it will still pick it up. But I guess the placement of the sensor here makes it very narrow, and to me that seems like an odd design flaw.

3 stars because it DOES work once you figure out how, but it is really not intuitive out of the box to expect others to use.

The good news is that it DOES work, and sounds pretty decent for a cheap no-name brand. If you've installed a double din stereo before, it should be pretty familiar and straight forward.
But let's just jump right into the odd design. Why is there an "external mic" option that is RIGHT NEXT to the internal mic? Usually an external mic is supposed to be mounted somewhere closer to the driver's mouth (up by the visor or mirror, or over the dash by the steering wheel, etc). The purpose is to get better sound, and either having the internal one as a backup if you don't want to mount one, or using it to pick up ambient background noise for NR filtering. Having an external nub right next to the internal one makes ZERO sense at all! Why even have one?! If anything, making it lower than the internal one seems like it would get WORSE sound, and if the position were so good, why not make THAT where the internal one is? Not to mention it looks weird as heck.
The features seem to be functional at least, but it has a pretty noticeable lag to the user interface. If you're expecting an OEM style menu experience, you might be disappointed. This feels like an old-school web browser loading pages when you open up a feature. Compared to modern units like, for example an Atoto F7, this feels like something a generation older at least.
I want to give this at least 3 stars for functional purposes, but the truth is I know that you get a much better unit for not a lot of money more. I can't really recommend it unless it is on an extreme sale.

This is a decent sounding pair of budget friendly wireless earbuds. They aren't the best for the price, but they aren't the worst either. They're about normal. But one of the big features of this set is supposed to be the touch controls, however my daughter found them completely unreliable. Sometimes she had to touch them 5x before they registered to pause the music, which made her more likely to pull out the player and pause it there instead.
I'd say these are 4 star headphones except for that selling point failure, if you are buying these because of the touch controls, I'd have to reduce the score to 3.

If you use a USB-C only laptop like a modern Mac, you need something like this to break out into display and USB A ports. I love how slim and functional the station itself is, it looks great on a desk next to a sleek laptop like a Macbook. However, it requires a large unsightly and clunky power brick to function. The brick is bigger than the whole docking hub!
You also can't use it without the brick, the unit needs its own power and does not get powered by the laptop. I understand the idea of a docking station is to charge the LAPTOP, but I've used smaller ones before that could either charge the laptop, or be used solo as just an adapter OTG for a USB stick to plug in. No such luck here, if the brick isn't plugged in, the hub won't turn on and none of the ports will work. For the price, I wasn't expecting that limitation.

This is a really solid idea for bloggers and others who want to mount camera and other recording equipment to their desk. I occasionally do video blog demonstrations and in my home office, that means setting up at least one light stand, a tripod with my camera, and a mic stand. Lots of stands on the floor taking up space.
With this, I can clamp the camera to my desk and use the crane arm to adjust- sounds great right?
Well- I'll be honest, this isn't designed to carry something like a DSLR or other ILC camera. Sure, I can get it to stay in place with some very delicate movements, but the slightest vibration and the camera wobbles which will show up in your video. I also am constantly afraid the balance will shift, I think this is better suited for a phone or gopro style camera.
In fact, I'm fairly certain this crane arm was NOT designed for this use at all. Something about it seemed familiar, and then I recognized it- it is the same desk clamp that came with one of my condenser mics, and I found it even has the 5/8" standard mic thread on the end! Basically, someone took a mass-produced microphone desk clamp and threw in some extra bits to adapt a tripod screw (1/4 20 thread) or phone holder mount to a microphone standard sized 5/8 end. That's it! This kit doesn't even come with instructions so you have to figure it out, but I could honestly have put this together with equipment I already owned if I knew that's all it was. I was hoping it would be a heavier duty product to hold my larger camera.

Oh well. It is still useful because I can mount a light to the 1/4" thread and use my other desk clamp to the hold the mic, thus leaving only my camera on the floor tripod. That's handy, but I can't give this more than 3 stars. I wish I could give 2.5, it's useful enough that it's not worth only 2 but 3 is being generous. Seems like a good idea that was thrown together without enough thought in the details.

UPDATE 1/2/22:
I CANNOT RECOMMEND THIS PLAYER. My kid changed the password on the lock screen and then immediately forgot what it is, locking everyone out of the player. No big deal, right? Just hard reset the whole device and start over... except that there is NO WAY TO PERFORM A HARD RESET. You must be logged in and have access to the settings screen to reach the reset settings, if you are locked out you have exactly ZERO options.
I reached out to support, and they offered to send me files to flash and reset the device, but then realized there is no way to get into the bootloader for me. Rather than offer a replacement, they offered 40% off purchasing another. No thank you, that's a terrible design flaw. Avoid this product.

Original review:
This is a cute little media player that is clearly powered by Android under the hood. It is NOT a phone or tablet, it does NOT have the Play store... it is very much designed to be strictly a media player. However unlike other cheap mp3 devices which struggle to make their own UI, these guys took the short cut and decided not to re-invent the wheel, rather opting to use the open-source and readily available Android operating system to handle the interface. And let me tell you, that makes it GREAT!
No more struggling to find an archaic avi codec to make videos work like other players, no more learning how to navigate a backwards menu system, or finding out that certain bluetooth devices or wifi networks are incompatible... no, this has all the support that the Android platform does, and it does it smoothly and quite well! It even has one of my favorite mp3 playing apps, AIMP preinstalled! Nice!
If you wanted to use this for more than just the included functionality, you CAN side-load Android APK files to install new applications. I did that to put a few cute games on it, but major apps that are closely tied to Google services such as Youtube and Gmail will not work. But that shouldn't be expected, this is a media player after all that happens to run a popular OS under the hood. I really like it, and most importantly, so do my kids who I got it for!

This is a great toy for a kid who's interested in science! It's essentially a kid's digital camera that can record stills and FHD video onto a memory card, however you can pick either a macro lens (microscope) or telephoto (telescope) with the press of a button. I thought this would be more interesting than the stand-alone microscope option, however now that I've tried it, I think the microscope is a better product. The telescope isn't all that useful- for starters, at the sort of telephoto distance you'd use here, it's nearly impossible to hold the thing still enough to avoid a blurry photo or shaky video. Also, the white balance is ridiculous and seems to lock onto the K-value of sunlight only, making everything just look bad.
The macro Microscope, on the other hand, is really nice. The end of the lens barrel lights up with LEDs to illuminate your subject, and that ensures the color white is really white as well. Also at short distance, it is easier to hold it still and you can get some really interesting pictures and videos of things so magnified as to make it seem like something else entirely.
Switching between the modes isn't all that intuitive, my kids seem to have trouble swapping them every time. The unit also doesn't have the highest build quality, feels like a cheap plastic kids camera. For the price, I was hoping for something a little bit better.
That being said, my daughter loves the microscope part and wants to take it to school to show her teacher. She has thanked me multiple times for it. I can't complain too much, she has fun with it and it does work. I just know it COULD have been better.

I'm very conflicted writing this review. As music listening and noise cancellation devices, they are wonderful! You can wear this in a noisy environment and get lost in your own tunes or just hear yourself think. Also, it has a similar functional design as Air Pods that allows air in to make it comfortable to wear without the vacuum "under water" seal effect that other ear buds have. So out of the box, color me impressed- comfortable and sounds great, what could be better, right?
Well, the reason I wanted to try Jabra over other brands is their commitment to call quality. Back in the early days of Bluetooth, Jabra was one of the kings if you wanted to ensure a clear 2-way conversation on a call. A lot of portable audio devices these days overlook mic quality and put all their effort into music / playback, with Apple, Sony, and some other big brands being the exception.
Sadly, these Jabras don't seem to deliver in that regard. People we call constantly complain they can't hear us, that we sound far away, under water or over-compressed / missing parts of our voice. In quiet environments it seems to work ok, but maybe the noise cancellation bit is working overtime? I don't know. All I know is I'm so disappointed with the call quality, I can't rely on these if I want the other party to hear me clearly. Yes, the ANC is awesome. Yes, the music sounds good. Yes they are comfortable. But if you need to switch to another headset to make a phone call, these are silly. I really wish it wasn't so.

I wanted to like this mouse. There are so many things I like about it better than my other wireless mouse- the design is more ergonomic and comfortable to hold, the buttons are easy to reach (if you're a righty at least!), and I like that it doesn't have a glowing red dot on the bottom, I'm assuming it uses IR or something invisible to humans. Although, to be fair, it does make it hard to determine if the thing is powered on or not!
At first I loved it, the scroll wheel is good, even the modes to control the dpi were a pleasure to cycle through. But then it got... jumpy. Like, sometimes I would move the mouse and it would feel like it paused and had to catch up all of the sudden. Movements didn't seem to mimic mine in real time. I do a lot of video editing and have to shuffle clips around with precise movements, I found this inconsistent behavior really unsettling to work with and needed to go back to me old boring flat mouse. If you don't have a mouse or just want to make browsing easier on a chromebook or something like that, it's good in a pinch, especially for the price. But sadly it is not reliable enough for moderate to heavy users in my opinion.

I wanted to upgrade my 04 Solara stock radio to one with bluetooth and a backup camera, but the car has a JBL factory amp and I wanted to keep this install as simple as possible (especially including steering wheel controls). Crutchfield recommended this model to make that happen, but it was out of stock so I ordered it here instead.
Well, for starters it only supports control over L+R, fading from front front to rear isn't an option as it just sends both front and back speakers the same signal. That's fine for a limitation, I did read that from the description here so I wasn't surprised, but it was just the first sign of a product that seems half baked. Next up, the steering wheel controls DID NOT WORK. I have an Atoto head unit, and none of the dip switch SWC settings worked. You have to set the buttons on the Atoto, but no matter what switch settings I used, I only got SOME of the buttons working and not others. Like, sometimes only vol + but not vol -, or a different setting gave me just mode and track down, but never all of them at once. I reached out to customer support and it took several tries to get a response, after which they gave me a different set of switch settings to try (not one from the manual) which still didn't work.
In the end, I cut the SWC wires from the harness and fed them directly to SW1 and SW2 on the Atoto harness directly, and got them ALL to show up and set correctly! So basically, buying the model with SWC retention was a waste of extra money as it didn't even work.
Then I had some ground loop noise I was trying to troubleshoot. To be fair, it could have been the radio, so I tried wiring it directly to speakers to see if the output from the radio had it... it did not. Another weird issue is that I noticed a faint hiss coming from the speakers EVEN WHEN THE RADIO WAS POWERED OFF. As in, I'm not playing anything and want the car to be dead silent, but the adapter still turned on the amp even if the head unit is off! It was more pronounced when I had ground loop noise, but now that I've mostly fixed that, there is still an obvious hum like there is power going to the amp and it is waiting for sound. This should power it off if my radio is off, but that is not happening. I reached out to Crux again, multiple times, explaining the problem and got no response. I reached out again and asked if I could just buy another wire harness in case there is something wonky about the one I have (the swc issue I later realized might have been one of the wires not communicating to the adapter, since connecting only sw1 or sw2 at a time made it act the way it did before with only half the buttons working at a time- but obviously my wire to the car was working as was the headunit because different settings switched around which buttons were active... so the fault must have been in the adapter or harness). No response. It was too late to return it so I tried troubleshooting on my own.

I'm living with the faint hiss for now, when the car is on it isn't a big deal and usually I'm listening to something anyway so that's fine. The fade from front to back is fine because its a coupe and not like there's a lot of difference between the front and rear of the car. The SWC buttons are working because I bypassed the faulty operation of the Crux unit, so it's mostly fine now. But I feel like I overpaid for something that under delivered. I wish I had gone with a different interfacing adapter and/or bypassed my factory amp. This was supposed to make the installation EASY and it ended up causing me more grief instead.
Also? Crux customer support has been terrible. When they did finally respond, it seemed like they didn't want to help because I didn't buy it from one of their authorized retailers and I wasn't a professional installer. Their website also went down for weeks in the middle and I feared they went out of business due to the pandemic. They have since responded so I know they are still around, but were not really helpful. The technical team at Atoto was worlds more helpful (they wanted it to work and were trying everything to see if the problem was on their side). It seems the problem was with Crux's adapter and their lack of support.

[[VIDEOID:2212eb120f801d8851a76eb4e94985a0]] This is a really cool way to make your head unit act like a tablet. If you have Android Auto in your dash, you already know that it is pretty cool but a watered down experience of the full blown OS on your phone. It also relies on your phone being plugged in. This device eliminates that by having its own complete Android operating system on a stick that appears on your display, completely independent of your phone. Complete with play store and streaming apps! It is a very cool concept and pretty useful, but sadly I hit some snags along the user experience:
1) You have to wait 30 seconds for it to boot every time you start the car.
2) Unlike Android Auto on your phone, you need to supply an internet connection (you can use your phone as a hotspot if your plan allows and you have enough data, but it is extra steps involved every time you boot if you want to connect)
3) There is no shutdown/sleep. When you turn off the car, the device abruptly dies and has to start fresh again each time. Aside from the long boot up each time, this leads to two potential problems:
3a)The time/date resets every time you turn the ignition. If you don't have a network connection for it to grab the correct time, it will default to thinking it is Dec 31st and 7am. Every. Single. Boot.
3b) Anyone who knows how operating systems work can vouch that if you are in the middle of a write operation (saving a file, updating an app, etc) storage could become corrupted if power is immediately shut without warning to the device. There is no warning to the device, it's either on while the car is, or dead when the ignition is cut. Heck, even if you leave the ignition in the acc position so it remains powered on, if you turn to the ignition position, that momentary cut to the power while the car starts means another 30 second reboot and the time reset to 7am. Very annoying.
4) There is no pinch to zoom option, which some apps (like maps) assume is available for the user experience.
5) Bluetooth support from a phone is very poor. The unit can tell you that a call is coming in, but you can't answer or initiate the call without exiting the UI and either going back to the head unit menu, or controlling it from the phone. Also, no phone audio (A2DP) is played from the phone because the MStick is using the Bluetooth profile for its own audio.

In a nutshell, a lot of these caveats could be worked around with some design changes. The stick could be built with a small internal battery much like a phone or tablet, so that it can sleep when the power is shut off and wait for the user to turn the car back on without rebooting from scratch. This would also solve the time reset issue.
The same way that there is a button on the nav bar to pull down the notification shade, there could be a button to enable pinch zooming within apps that require it.

There could also be a built in way to attach another display, perhaps mirror to a phone or remote desktop in so that you can set up all your apps, etc, at home in the comfort of your wifi instead of doing all of this outside in the car. Everytime I wanted to try something, I had to tinker outside in my driveway and run down my car's battery and/or waste fuel keeping it running for no reason. Little things like that would make a HUGE difference in the end user experience. This product seems like more hassle than it is worth for the average user, but is an excellent proof of concept if you want to, for example, have Torque running on your car display but not upgrade the whole stereo to an Android powered one.
BUT, then again, it sort of begs to wonder why not just get an Android tablet or old phone and mount it on the dash and leave the radio to connect with your phone? The user experience might be better than working around the caveats that this introduces.

I understand the need to have a dedicated media player at times. However, much like others I have used, this uses a very barebones UI that is laggy and feels very outdated compared to a smart device. The font has hard lines that are sometimes hard to read, and occasionally you'll even meet elements of the UI that have parts written in Chinese characters. And the video playback option is a joke- you can only play videos in a specific codec that is archaic and unreliable (and needs a bizarre app to encode to).
It has an Fm tuner which is nice, and the size is super portable and cute. And honestly, this would be a decent device if I didn't know that for around the same price you can get much more polished media players powered by a modified smartphone OS. For example, another media player that I recently tried actually had a linux/Android kernel running under the hood, but stripped of all the smartphone parts. It supported video playback of modern formats, had more more pleasing fonts and a UI that was fast and responsive. I mean, in this day and age, unless this were half the price, there's no excuse for a UI to feel so far behind.

Ok, first of all, I want to say I LOVE this player much more than others I've used. My kids are not allowed cell phones in school, but they are allowed music players- however most players that aren't smart devices are really janky with buggy/slow UIs and lots of impairments (I tried encoding a video for one and it wouldn't work unless I used a very archaic codec that required a suspicious Chinese desktop app). This, however, actually runs a stripped down version of Android under the hood. This is a GOOD thing! The UI is very polished and smooth thanks to open source mature OS, and features like video playback are much more robust with a wider variety of formats supported and compatible as a result as well!
The hardware is smooth and the menus are intuitive thanks to being familiar with the Android OS already. It's a very cute device!
So why only 3 stars? Well, the listing claims it has a web browser and FM radio. Both of those things are missing on this model. The truth is, I don't need my kids to have that anyway, but it feels weird that the listing advertises features which aren't there. I think I may have gotten a different model than the one advertised.
I considered side-loading a browser apk since it DOES run android, but the truth is this isn't designed for that sort of use and wouldn't make a difference for the purpose of this review. I'd imagine that there are a lot of possible hacks and modifications possible thanks to the operating system inside if someone wanted to tinker.

There are dozens if not hundreds of off-brand Android tablets available these days. Some of them are impressive for the money, some of them have stand-out features like USB host ports, removable batteries or IR blasters... and some of them are just boring run-of-the-mill standard fare. This is one of the latter ones, unfortunately.
The screen size is nice at 10", but the resolution is a paltry 720p at that size, which makes the pixels more noticeable on fine text and graphics. If all you want is something to play games and watch videos on, the display is fine, but if you want the large screen for an e-reader or for pixel-peeping details in graphics, the resolution will quickly feel too low. The processor is not terribly fast, although it holds up decently if you're not multitasking a lot. That being said, the 2GB of RAM won't hold up to a lot of multitasking anyway. The cameras are pretty terrible, too. If you need a device for a zoom meeting and having good lighting, having a bad camera is better than no camera, but don't expect to take pictures worth keeping. Like, at all. Pictures look almost like old flip-phone era quality. And beyond that, there are no stand out features that add value to it. There's a TF slot, but that's not rare. Supposedly there is a SIM slot, however there is a lot of conflicting info in the paperwork re: whether this device is WiFi only, and I wasn't able to determine any cellular functionality.
At the end of the day, it's a good bargain tablet with a decent sized display. You can do basic Android tasks, play some light games, watch some videos, etc, and if that's all you want it for, it'll get the job done. BUT... keep in mind that there are alternatives like the Kindle Fire and brands like Lenovo's M10 which are pretty close to the asking price on this and have a far superior user experience. So it sort of makes one wonder why someone would choose this device over those. If you can get this for significantly less than those models (perhaps if it goes on sale), I'd recommend it as a toss around tablet. But the value is really hard to find at the moment.

These are great for removing the clutter that comes from traditional PC speakers. Personally, I'm tired of the mess that my home editing/gaming PC speakers take: A right and left speaker with a cable connecting them, a cable with a 3.5mm jack to go into the back of the computer case, and then another cable to go into the outlet for power. It's just a mess of wires and really makes me miss my old Macintosh from the early 90s that had integrated speakers inside the case.
I was thinking about trying to wire up a DIY dynamic speaker inside my case, when I discovered this listing on Amazon. It essentially is a USB sound card built into a small stereo speaker array. All powered off the USB port. So you need one, single USB cable, no multiple wires back and forth, and no more giant wall adapter on my power strip! It actually is pretty cute on my desk, doesn't take up a lot of space, and has an integrated volume dial. Awesome!
The only catch? The sound isn't so great. And when that's the purpose of the product, you have to be a little upset about it. I have portable Bluetooth speakers that sound much clearer than this. It's not that it doesn't get loud (it totally can), but the clarity is lacking, as is the bass (in a major way). It's hard to describe- it's louder than a phone, but still has that tin sounding quality I'd expect from a speakerphone. Not exactly high quality. I wouldn't watch a movie or use it for atmospheric game soundscapes, but if you have a home PC and don't want to wear headphones or clutter up your desk with lots of wires, the single USB connection is pretty nice.

[[VIDEOID:2e1e48afafe7261f888f4fa063c2dbdd]] I really like the fact that this is a larger display than the 7 inchers you usually find in car radio replacements. That's what initially attracted me to trying this unit, since my Toyota Solara's double din dash kit has tons of unused space to the right and left of the faceplate. The problem?
It's *slightly* too large vertically, and is centered instead of starting at the bottom. To explain: I measured my dashboard and realized it would stick up past the top and partially cover the bottom of my hazard button as well as the vents, but that's livable. I don't use the hazard button very often, and the vents can be adjusted away from it. The problem is, it sticks out both top AND bottom, with the middle double-din sized part being centered in the display. That downward part concerns me because of my ability to turn the knobs for the climate control underneath. I wish that the unit started at the bottom of the double-din space and only went UP only. That's what I was expecting it to do, the way modern car radios have displays that stick out vertically but are flush with the dash underneath. I'm not ok with it rubbing against the climate knobs.
I took a video of trying to install it on my dash kit before I gave up and put it back in the box. I DID hook it up to 12v power just to see it turn on and make sure everything works, and I have to say it's a shame because this LOOKS really cool. I love that it runs Android and has all the customization I'd crave from a system like that. Android Auto is a treat too. I didn't hook up any speakers so I can't vouch for sound quality and I can't vouch for the longevity of the unit since I didn't actually keep it in my car, but it looks like a pretty good value for the money if this fits your dash layout.

I have an mp3 player that has only a USB-C port. It came with USB-C headphones as well as a 3.5mm adapter for regular headphones that we promptly lost.

I really wanted this to replace those, however I tried with several pairs of headphones and NONE of them had sound using this adapter. It detected that headphones were connected, but no sound came out. Very disappointed.

I found that these charge easily and hold their charge well enough to play for a long time... however they don't lock into the stock Xbox 360 controller that well. I found one of them did better than the other, but even then it didn't really feel "clicked in". I had to play with it before it clicked on finally and it seems to be working fine now. However it shouldn't be so difficult to get it working. Beats changing batteries with disposables, but still- I think you can find better ones that will lock in properly.

I have an HP laptop I want to use in the field for running an all-day event stream without needing to tether to a wall. I thought something like this would be a good move to keep it charged since the battery only lasts about 2.5 hours running the stream (it's CPU intensive). However, this laptop does not support USB-C PD charging unfortunately (I was hoping it did, there is a USB-C port, but sadly only output is supported), so I had to resort to using the AC part. Now, I know converting DC from a battery to AC requires quite a bit of power loss, but one recharge of my laptop from single digits to 80% practically wiped the power supply out. I definitely would not be able to charge the laptop more than once off of this, and I have my doubts it would even make it all the way to 100% without dying honestly. I was really hoping it would last longer. If you have a PD-compatible laptop, this might work better for you. I DO love that it has an AC outlet for emergencies, and I'll probably take this with us camping because it is pretty cool to have. But the product description implies this is a good option for charging a laptop, but for the price I've seen better options I think. At the very least, I wish this had a automotive-style 12v DC port so I could try getting that kind of charger for my laptop (less power lost since not inverting to AC), but alas. The only real laptop charging options are AC and USB-C/PD, and if your laptop doesn't use the latter, the first is a pretty inefficient option.

I wasn't expecting this to be a speed demon, it says right on the box USB2 so I knew I wasn't going to get the 150+MB/s level speeds I get with some of my thumb drives. But even for USB2, this is on the slow side. Plugging in a standard sandisk drive to my USB2 port, I'm able to pull over 40MB/s without breaking a sweat. This one? Even on a USB3 port, I'm only able to pull a bit over 18MB/s in read, and the writing is even more abysmal. That's less than half of what USB2 can pull.
For the money, this is a decent delivery platform for you to hand off large files to someone, or perhaps to play media on a USB TV or something like that. But for regular daily transfer of data, you might find this painfully slow. As you can see in the benchmark screenshot attached, it timed out for the last two write tests and never even finished.

I listen to lectures on headphones when doing chores around the house and often can't hear people trying to get my attention. I've seen neck speakers before, and I thought it would be a very cool option for me as my family gets kind of annoyed that I can't hear them and they can't tell if I'm currently listening to something.
But I'll be honest, after trying these, I'm not really loving them. I had a pair of sunglasses speakers that aimed sound towards my ears, but this sort of blasts sound out and around me. Like, not even towards my ears. Basically, it seems just as loud to someone else in the room with me as it does to me, which then begs the question of why not just use an external speaker at that point? The call quality was just OK as well. The one thing I can say is that the build quality seems quite good. It feels really durable and made with premium feeling materials. But I just can't shake the feeling that for the asking price, I'm missing the point of these. Shouldn't the speakers be facing upwards towards my ears instead of blasting at each other in front of my Adam's Apple? Seems like a weird design that might be missing the mark.

I thought I'd want a bigger cover for my 10" Lenovo tab, but this was too much. It made the tablet feel heavy and bogged down, difficult to hold easily to read. That totally defeated the purpose for me, so I'm actually planning on returning it as soon as a simpler and thinner model arrives. The way the back is attached means it's basically double thickness, and the extra flap in the cover adds a cool aesthetic but also makes it double as thick. Compared to my Samsung Galaxy tablet with a foldable flip cover, this is like 3x the width, not to mention feels odd to hold open in my hands in comparison.
Some people might like this style, but it's not for me.

I'm glad I tested this card before using it on something in my camera. I don't know where they come off trying to call this "professional" in the title, but this is anything but. The speeds are atrocious, attaching a benchmark to show. This is no where near the claims of U3, or 1000x or 95mbs. As you can see, I'm barely getting 18 reading. And the test actually locked up for the last two items. I tried it again and played the settings and finally got it to complete the test, but the card seems super unreliable and too slow for 4K video caputre, possibly even too slow for decent 1080 codecs as well.
The capacity is also reported oddly- my Sandisk cards (which I tested right after this to make sure the equipment wasn't faulty), not only tested approximately to the speed printed on the card in benchmarks, but it reports a 64GB card is around 60 after formatting. This one says 62 after formatting, which makes me wonder if the capacity is fake and being incorrectly reported by the chip inside. This card seems too good to be true for a reason, I would not trust it.

I knew this was a USB 2.0 drive, but this is slow even for that standard. I tried using it to copy the contents of a memory card over to another computer that didn't have a card reader, and it was frustrating. 32GB (half the capacity of the card) took about 2 hours to write! Playing it back was OK, but doing a benchmark speed test I can see that even the read speed is well below the USB 2.0 standard.
It works, so I'm giving it 3 stars, but I can't think of an opportunity that I would want to use this for the intended capacity. Can you imagine needing 4 hours to copy over the entire 64GB capacity of the card? No thank you!

This is basically a USB host cable that delivers power, and a mini USB hub with Ethernet built in. I wish I could review them separately because the USB host part works perfectly! I tried it on several devices (including my Moto G5 Plus smartphone) and it gives everything a USB port to plug a peripheral into. I wanted this for my Amazon FireStick 4k, which was successfully given a USB port which can be used for things like game controllers and wireless keyboard/mouse combos, etc.
The USB hub + Ethernet works alright- the USB ports, at least, work fine. I'm able to plug in a keyboard and wireless controller adapter dongle, and everything works fine and is recognized by the Firestick. You can even plug in a USB storage stick to play local content. But I REALLY wanted the Ethernet port to get a stronger connection by the TV for streaming. I know there are other USB host / ethernet combos that work with the FireStick, it is capable of working with the right hardware. I thought this would be one of them since it claims to be "for Streaming TV Stick" in the description, however the Ethernet port does NOT work. I'll have to try to source my own and see if I can use it with the USB host this offers. The Ethernet port did show up on my Windows desktop when I tried the hub there, so maybe it just isn't compatible with Android/non desktops? I don't know. If that's the feature you want, this might not work for you.

This has so much potential, but just barely falls short of what I want in a media center remote. I have a fire stick 4k attached to a TV, and while the stock IR remote it came with is close to everything I need (can do TV's volume and power thanks to pre-programmed IR), it lacks a keyboard and programmable buttons (my stereo system isn't in the Fire TV's list so it can't control it, and I use that for surround sound). I have a USB host adapter that allows me to use media keyboard combos like this one on the stick, so I could have my QWERTY but traditionally then I'd give up the Alexa mic and IR controls of the stock remote since they usually don't have that. Whats amazing about this is that on paper I should still have everything I love- a QWERTY on one side, nav pad and plenty of shortcut buttons on the flip side, programmable IR buttons (YES!), and even a voice assistant mic button!
Seems too good to be true, because it sort of it. The mic button doesn't seem to work on Fire stick or even on my old Chinese Android player box. In Windows it seems to launch Cortana but I don't use that. Maybe it does something on Apple TV like invoke Siri, but I don't have one to test. The button in my case, is useless. Also, the programmable IR buttons? I was able to train the buttons to my TV for power and vol + and -. but not the stereo system. Sometimes it would seem to work and remember one side (either volume up or down) but never both together. I'd clear the buttons to default and start over, and then the TV ones wouldn't work either (commence tearing out hair). After a few cycles attempted to learn my IR codes, I got the TV working again but never the entire stereo system. What stinks is that I can already do that on my stock Firestick remote, and at least there I also get working Alexa voice command via the same remote. This didn't do that properly. Also on the firestick, system android volume settings don't effect anything. So I really wanted to reprogram the vol up and down buttons to the IR codes, but I could only do that on one of the 4 programmable buttons.

The air mouse function is really useful, and having the full keyboard is cool and good to have, but sadly this isn't that much better than the cheaper standard USB or BT keyboards you could already hook up and lose the voice input and IR control. You still need both, and in my case also the remote for the surround sound. I was hoping to consolidate all of those into one unit, and this really COULD have been the one to bring them all together if it was designed better.

I wanted to use these to replace some older bookshelf speakers in our living room, currently connected to a streaming Alexa-enabled player. I like that these have two auxiliary inputs so technically I can attach it to our audio system and ALSO something like our home theater receiver, and occasionally use Bluetooth to connect to a phone when needed. These are much nicer looking and sound really good compared to my old speakers, however I'm rather annoyed that everytime they power up it defaults to Bluetooth again. My audio system gets shut off at night and turned back on in the morning via a switch. I really wish the speakers would go back to the last setting used, or perhaps have a way to change the default. As it is right now, every morning we have to find the remote and press Line 1 to hear the music, despite the player trying to play. Even worse, if we can't find the remote, there's NO WAY to change settings on speaker itself. This just seems like an unnecessary extra step and it has made some of my family members prefer the old speakers instead, sadly.
It is very unfortunate because these otherwise have the potential to be so incredible! But this is a usability fail. It should at the very least recall the last mode used.

I got excited to see one of these small portable LED style ones that actually had a decent native resolution (most of them can accept 1080p, but are in reality only 800x600 resolution, or sometimes worse... 640x480!). This one is actually capable of displaying 720p of real dot resolution, which should make it at least as sharp as my Viewsonic and other traditional HD projectors. Ok, perhaps I'm spoiled, but I'm comparing this to our Viewsonic 720p projector that, to be fair cost me 3-4x as much.
And for the most part, it DOES work, however there are some caveats to its use. First of all, it doesn't seem as sharp as my 720p projector, even though it should have the requisite amount of dots. It's OK, its definitely better than the cheap 600p projectors, but something just isn't quite there when comparing side by side. It also doesn't get all that bright, but I suppose that's expected from the LED tech being used. You'll need black out shades or use it only during the night. Then there's the color- it isn't great. It works, but it has a cheap color reproduction that looks kind of flat and lifeless. Dark scenes sort of all blend together and become nearly impossible to see. It lacks the vibrancy of even an inexpensive television from decades ago. It gets the job done, but hardly the "theater experience" if you've been waiting to see that latest action/vfx film the way it was intended. It will look better on your TV at home, the only thing this has going for it is the large projection experience. For example, if you just want to give your kids a backyard movie night and don't care that the color and detail won't be as great as your indoor system, it will do the job on the cheap. I personally would not give up my mid-range projector for this one.
One thing that I found particularly annoying is that rather than the optical zoom and focus dials found on usual projectors, there is only a focus and tilt dial. No zoom. That means you have to physically move the projector closer or further to get it to reach the correct size you are shooting for. This is a smartwatch running Google's Wear OS. My wife does love it, but we have some reservations with recommending it. Before we go any further, I'd like to point out that most of our qualms have to do with Wear OS itself, so it would be true of any smartwatch running that system.
Let me start off by saying this watch is really very pretty and my wife LOVES the styling of it. Before this she was using more utility-looking fitness bands like those from Xiaomi and FitBit. Her last band, a Mi Band 3, was great for functionality, but she found it ugly. This one she actually really likes, and features like apps, the full color touch screen, custom watch faces, programmable buttons, and dial to control menus really showcases the difference between a proper "smartwatch" and the cheaper activity trackers she is used to. It feels and looks undeniably cool.
But after a week or two of using it, there are some things that we really wish were different about it. For starters, the battery life is pretty terrible. On days that she uses it a lot (like when we first got it), it seems to need to be charged before the day is over. After settling into a routine and changing to a very basic watch face, and also turning off features like wake on wrist detection, we are able to last at least 24 hours to maybe a day-and-a-half on a charge. In other words, even with pretty conservative battery usage, you can easily make it the entire day but still need to charge it daily because it definitely won't make it through that second day. That means when we go away for a weekend, its another charger that has to come with us. I see that this is unfortunately normal for Wear OS devices, as 1-2 days of battery is the average even from other brands running Google's smartwatch OS. To contrast, my wife's Mi Band 3 went for nearly 3 weeks on a charge, which meant she could wear it 24-7 and get the benefits of things like sleep tracking with it. This can't really do that well. To be fair, my friends with other smartwatches (Apple, Samsung, etc) say they have to charge it daily as well, so perhaps this is an expected compromise for users preferring smartwatches to bands and other trackers.
The next thing, and this is sort of a recent sore point it seems, the pedometer and step goals have been replaced with "heart points" thanks to a very new partnership between Google and the American Heart Association. They decided that counting steps isn't good enough, and came up with a different calculation for activity and setting goals for it. This is all fine and good, except that they DON'T HAVE THE OPTION TO SET STEP GOALS. I guess in an effort to get everyone interested in the new system, they are almost trying to hide the pedometer functions of Google Fit. In order to get your steps you have to find them buried in a menu, and there's no current watch face that will show you real-time steps that I could find. Oh, and did I mention you can't set it as a goal anymore? This is very frustrating as my wife and I use steps competitively as do many work place initiatives and similar programs... this is a basic function that EVERY activity tracker lets you do! Everything from the cheapo Chinese trackers to the name brands, to the Apple watches, to even Google Fit as of a few months ago! I looked up ways to bring the pedometer functions back into front and center and found many tirades on the internet from disgruntled users who also wanted the feature back. I get it, the heart points is probably better, but at least let US, as users, choose!
At the end of the day, my wife and I find it very awkward that this higher priced smartwatch, with all of its high end features and wow factors, can't handle the simple things that her cheaper Mi Band did great- the old band showed us her steps on the main display with the time, in real time, and would need to be charged about once monthly. But to be fair, now that she's been spoiled by the style and ability to respond to text messages from the watch (the band only showed them, you couldn't respond to them), she's not planning on going back. I'm hoping that Google's Wear OS addresses some of these issues in the future and/or Fossil themselves address it. They could, for example, design a device with better battery and a custom Fossil watch face that still does step counting. But this doesn't. So for us, the experience doesn't seem to match the price point. IF you like Wear OS and are already aware of its limitations in battery and pedometer, this is a very nice option.

This is a good product, but perhaps not exactly what I was expecting it to be. I was hoping to conceal two different things- a floor lamp cord, and a cat5 cable along a wall. For a single cable run like a power plug or a measly cat5 cable, it seems absurdly wider than the cable it is concealing.
That other thing I found interesting is that one of the walls I wanted to use it on isn't completely straight. A handyman had helped me repair a wall and paint it, and now I see it has a slight curve to it which I wasn't able to notice before. The covers don't sit entirely flat against the wall, which just sort of looks awkward around the ever-so-slightly-curved portion unless I fill it in with spackle. I could overlook all these things and say perhaps my test usage are uncommon scenarios, except for one final thing: the adhesive is TOO good!
If you decide you don't like it / want it, and used the adhesive instead of the screws, you are going to rip a lot of the wall off with the cover when you remove it. I wasn't sure if this was just me, but I see from other reviews that they claim pieces of the drywall were coming off with the paint, which is quite frankly somewhat horrifying if you didn't know it would do that. I still have the paint for this wall so I'm not concerned, but I'd strongly recommend using the screws if you have the option and don't want this to be a permanent fixture in your home.

UPDATE: I noticed that my setup would start displaying an incorrectly sized and formatted hdmi feed (instead of 1920x1080, it was a squashed 960x1080 with incorrect colors). If I turned the whole system off and wait a few minutes before turning back on, it would sometimes go away but it is very strange. I thought it was either the player or projector connected to it for months now, but I just did some testing and realized it has been this HDMI extender! A monitor plugged into the source displayed fine, and plugged into this receiver had the same 960x1080 w/ mixed up colors that my projector did. The good news is that the transmitter has a reset button and that seems to fix it when it happens. But it sometimes comes back when I reboot or start up from everything being off. It is annoying that I have to go find the little reset button because the transmitter is hidden in a cabinet, and it seems like a completely unnecessary step to take every time I boot up. Hoping Sabrent can offer a solution- if so I'll update my review back to 5 stars because otherwise this is excellent.
These things are a great way to reliably reach farther than an HDMI cable, but you need to still understand the limitations. Video requires a lot of bandwidth, so the quality and length of your cable is directly related to how realistic it is to reach the maximum resolution and frame rate.
I already have an older one of these from a different brand, which I bought a couple of years ago for a projector in the back of the room (switch between TV and projector, but entertainment system is in front of room and projector is in back, hence the need for a long run of cable). That older one claimed to work at 1080/60p, and in my initial tests it did. But once I ran the long cable, I was able to only get 720/60p or 1080 at only 24p. 1080 at 60 was just too much bandwidth and the adapter just couldn't handle it over a longer cable run.
This adapter, however, is rated at a higher spec for 4K. Swapping my old one out with this one, I'm happy to report that now I can get 1080 even at 60p from point to point. Could I get 4k at that length? I don't know, my projector doesn't handle 4k, but I'm guessing as the length of cable increases, it will limit what spec you can reliably expect. But I am very pleased with finally getting 1080p at this length of cable, so 5 stars!

It worked fine but was sometimes slow with downloading over WiFi, not surprising. From the research and reviews, and most importantly the price - we decided to try this Trendnet AC1750 router.

WOW what garbage - he no longer gets WiFi in his bathroom corner of the house - it is a VERY small 2 bedroom apartment. How in the world can this router not handle a signal from 20 feet away, with only 2 walls in between? A router of this caliber (even at this price) should EASILY be able to handle covering a 2 bedroom small apartment. Period.

I have tried updating firmware, all network resets I can. I've even tried using the old modem (we replaced both router + modem) to see if that was the root of our problems - nope, it's the router.

It has slowly been getting worse and worse, and when I am gone from this apartment my roommate will be forced to reset his router every day, sometimes twice a day, just to get internet - or purchase a new one.

I am extremely dissatisfied with this product, although not quite surprised or disappointed given its price. It just seems odd that a 3 year old Netgear N300 router performs much better than an AC1750 Dual Band router.

i really wish there was more space filled in between the high end garmin stuff and the entry level. this computer is really close to being good enough for me, but it lacks key abilities. here's what it would need to work for me personally:
standard file format - e.g. FIT, gpx, whatever.
easy access to data - even just as files on a drive via USB - i can automate data transfer from there
write power data to file
option to display zones and percentages for all data

that's all i would need from a barebones head unit for my own training and riding

Not a criticism of the particular product but of the grounding mechanism.

Beware of grounding mats. Long term use may cause discomfort, pain and even damage. It should be okay to use briefly, but not for any extended period of time.

This is due to the way energy circulates through the body. Extended use causes the gathering and accumulation of energy in certain areas. This is rarely discussed and relatively unknown to most people.

Another thing to consider- you are plugging yourself into your house's electrical grounding system. You have to make sure your house is properly grounded. Youd be surprised that some may not be. If you are in a building its even worse. Also, all sorts of pollutants travel through the grounding path. It doesnt travel just one way.

Grounding is more complicated than it appears so be aware. There are other ways to do it but its not as easy as just plugging yourself in I suppose. Hence the allure of these mats

I originally bought this camera at the same time as the Canon G15, in order to try both out, compare them, and choose one to keep for my own use. As it turned out, I had not yet made my final decision, but was leaning towards the Canon because of its faster speeds and somewhat sharper pics and better overall performance, when my husband stepped in and commandeered the Nikon. I was a little nonplussed by his move because there were a couple of features on this camera that surpassed the Canon and I was still on the fence about it. I very much like the vari-angle LCD on the Nikon, as well as the much farther reach of the zoom.

However, after owning and using both cameras since the beginning of April, I have to say that I am much happier with the Canon. And not so much just because of the advantages described above, but more because we have also had the dubious "opportunity" to compare the warranty service levels available to both cameras. And also, in no small way, because our Nikon is now systematically sucking dust into its layers of lenses. Yes, I said "into".

Here is the whole story of what happened with both cameras: A few months ago, after having taken a total of about 11,000 pics with the Canon, it started jamming up. I called Canon, explained the symptoms and was immediately (within less than half an hour) emailed the documentation I needed to fill out and a prepaid UPS label and instructions on how and where to send the camera back and how long it would take to repair and return it. All this was done exactly as described, and I didn't have to pay a penny out of my pocket. The camera arrived back within the appointed timeframe, functioning perfectly. However, when I got it back, I noticed a very tiny nick in the paint on the removable neck ring around the base of the lens barrel. I called and asked Canon to replace it, letting them know that my camera had been returned to them in 'like new' condition, so it had obviously been nicked while in their care. The person I reported this to, asked me to hold while he asked a supervisor how to proceed with this. The supervisor came on the line and recommended I send the camera back so they could check it through again, to make sure that whatever had caused the nick had not further damaged the camera somehow - as in a drop or jar of the camera. I was pretty sure that was not the case, but agreed to send it back and let them look it over just the same. I told them I was a bit upset at having to be without my camera for several more days again. They told me they would expedite things for the second round, so I wouldn't have to wait as long this time. They made good on that promise by sending me a UPS Overnight label to pick up the camera. They kept it for just a few days, but sent it back via UPS Ground Service, which was a bit of a letdown.

In contrast, when Nikon was called about the dust and bits of grass in the lens problem the first time, a couple of months ago, it took them a couple of days to send over the paperwork to fill out. Neither the paperwork nor their email contained any information about how long the repairs might take, and we also had to ship the camera back to them at our own expense. Not a huge expense, admittedly, but still a contrast to Canon's better efforts to keep customers happy.

Now, less than two months after getting the camera back, there are dust particles in the lens again. We live in Vermont and my husband uses the camera for street photography here and in Montreal. These places are not exactly known for being dust bowls... So, in effect, the camera has not been subjected to any unusual conditions. Yet the seals are clearly not doing their job because the camera is sucking foreign particles into its lens system at several different levels of the optics.

We reported the problem to Nikon last Friday, early afternoon, and they sent a preliminary email acknowledging that they have received our communication. Once again though, here it is Monday and we are still waiting for the necessary paperwork to be sent, so we can return the camera (at our expense again, even though it's the same problem they were supposed to have fixed last time and the camera is still under warranty...) and hopefully get it back before Christmas. A hope that was communicated to the Nikon rep when we called in to report this reoccurrence of the problem last Friday.

I would have given this camera a 4 star rating, had it not been for the contrast in the service level with the Canon people and, of course, the unacceptable seals that allow dust to be sucked into the optics of our camera. I have not seen any other people complaining about this problem, so I am assuming it is unique to our own camera. Once this problem is corrected to our satisfaction, I will update my review and the star rating too.

UPDATE: Nikon took the camera and did pay for the shipping this time, when we asked (Canon does it without asking, every time). They did not get the camera back to us before Christmas. When they returned the camera to us the first time, the camera started having issues with accepting third party batteries. Since they returned it this time, it has not been accepting third party batteries at all. Clearly, they have upgraded to their new firmware, which locks out third party batteries for not only this camera, but all Nikon cameras that use the EN-EL14 batteries. There is more info about this on the web. I will include a link in the comments section about this.

Aside from our 4 back-up batteries now not working in our camera, it is also behaving extremely erratically. It has been on one photo shoot so far. Took over 300 pics. Had several strange things happen. The camera stopped taking pics at one point. LCD working fine, button depressing, but no pic. Tried again, display info disappeared, still no pic. LCD showing the scene, but display info gone, button depressing properly, but the camera is not recording the shots. Camera will not turn off. Had to remove the battery to turn it off. After that, it started working again. When the pics were downloaded, several overlapped, some vertically (kind of looked like a film camera's pics would if you didn't wind the film properly all the way to the next frame), some horizontally, creating a weird, half 'n half effect. One picture showed up with a severe white balance issue. It was in a deep blue hue. The camera was being used in AWB the whole time.

We have some more experimenting to do with the pictures. We will load them onto a different computer, with a different program and see what we find. We will also be scrolling through the images directly on the SD card. Will report back when we have more info.

The little tabs lock it into the base so tight that when you try to flip it back up to do the alignment process it wont budge. I tried centering the mount in the base and pulled up with moderate force. The base broke in the same way that the original did when I struk something in the water. Ultimately I trimmed the little tabs slightly so that it will pup up with moderate force. Granted I may have nuisance popups. But that's better than being without the use of the sonar for several days.

I bought two. One for now to replace one that broke this week. Another for future use. Well I now know why the original broke. This mount has a speed breakaway feature in case you strike something with it. Well the tabs, that should allow the sendig unit to flip up when it strikes something, hold to the base so hard that the base breaks(away). I found this out while installing the new one today. During the trial fit part of the installation you need to engage the tabs to check for proper location of the sending unit. I needed to flip the sending unit up to make an adjustment. In doing so the base broke. I had to use great force to get it to flip up. I inspected the tabs on the sending unit part. They are so large that they would not allow the unit to "just" flip up as I would have expected. So when I install the backup mount I trimmed the tabs slightly so that the unit now flips up easier but with enough tension it should hold under speed.
